followups.a: Record a start index that resets whenever `cur` restarts from a[i], and capture both endpoints whenever `best` improves.

followups.q: Solve it with divide and conquer.
followups.a: Split in half; the answer is the best in the left, the best in the right, or the best crossing subarray computed by expanding outward from the midpoint. O(n log n) - worse, but it is the intended follow-up.

followups.q: The array is circular.
followups.a: Either the answer is a normal maximum subarray, or it wraps - in which case it is the total minus the MINIMUM subarray. Guard the all-negative case, where the second branch gives an empty subarray.

tuf.striver_title: Print the matrix in spiral manner

learnings.insight: There is no clever insight here and pretending otherwise wastes time. It is four boundary pointers and disciplined bookkeeping - the skill being tested is whether you can write fiddly index code correctly the first time.
learnings.trick: Keep top, bottom, left, right. Traverse right along top then top++, down the right then right--, and so on. Before the two reverse traversals, re-check `top <= bottom` and `left <= right` or a single remaining row or column is emitted twice.
edge_cases: Single row or single column - this is exactly what the mid-loop guards catch.
Non-square matrices are the common failure.
Stop when the output has m*n entries, or when the boundaries cross.

complexity.why: every cell is visited exactly once and the boundaries only shrink.

followups.q: Generate an n x n spiral rather than reading one.
followups.a: LC 59 - identical boundary logic, writing values 1..n^2 instead of reading.

followups.q: Why do the reverse traversals need an extra guard?
followups.a: After the two forward traversals the boundaries may already have crossed. Without the check, a single leftover row is read left-to-right and then again right-to-left.

learnings.insight: You never need to know HOW to reach an index, only whether it is reachable. That collapses a search over paths into a single running maximum of the furthest reachable position.
learnings.trick: Walk left to right maintaining `reach`. If ever i > reach you are standing beyond everything reachable, so return false. Otherwise update reach = max(reach, i + a[i]).
edge_cases: A zero at the final index is harmless - you only need to arrive there, not jump onward.
Single element is trivially true.
The check `i > reach` must come BEFORE updating reach, or an unreachable index updates the frontier.

complexity.why: one pass, one scalar. The DP version marking reachability per index is O(n^2) and is the solution this replaces.

followups.q: Work backwards instead.
followups.a: Track the leftmost index from which the end is reachable; move it left whenever i + a[i] >= lastGood. Equivalent, and some find it easier to justify.

followups.q: Jumps may go in both directions.
followups.a: That is LC 1306 and it stops being greedy - it becomes BFS or DFS over a graph, because reachability is no longer monotone in the index.

learnings.insight: Once intervals are sorted by start, any interval can only overlap the one immediately before it in the output. That reduces an all-pairs overlap problem to a single linear sweep.
learnings.trick: Sort by start. For each interval, either extend the last output interval's end with max(), or append a new one. The max() is essential - a later interval may be entirely contained within the current one.
edge_cases: Fully contained intervals - without max() you shrink the end and lose coverage.
Touching intervals [1,3] and [3,5] merge under <=; use < if touching should not merge.
Single interval returns itself; empty input returns empty.

complexity.why: the sort dominates; the sweep is linear. Sorting by start is what makes one comparison per interval sufficient.

followups.q: Insert one interval into an already-sorted list.
followups.a: LC 57 - O(n) without sorting. Emit everything ending before the new one, merge the overlapping run, then emit the rest.

followups.q: Find the free gaps rather than the merged intervals.
followups.a: Merge first, then the gaps are the spaces between consecutive merged intervals.

followups.q: Why sort by start rather than end?
followups.a: Merging needs positional adjacency. Sorting by end is for scheduling - maximising a count of non-overlapping intervals - which is a different problem.

learnings.insight: The input is already sorted, so sorting again wastes the free information. The list splits cleanly into three regions - before, overlapping, after - and each is handled by its own loop.
learnings.trick: Phase 1: emit every interval ending before the new one starts. Phase 2: absorb every overlapping interval into the new one by taking min of starts and max of ends, then emit it. Phase 3: emit the rest unchanged.
edge_cases: The new interval may overlap nothing and belong at either end.
It may swallow every existing interval.
Empty input returns just the new interval.

complexity.why: one pass over the sorted input with no sort. Sorting first would be O(n log n) and throws away the precondition.

followups.q: Many insertions rather than one.
followups.a: Repeated O(n) insertion is O(n*k). Better to collect them all and merge once, or keep the set in a std::map keyed by start for O(log n) insertion.

followups.q: Why three loops instead of one with branches?
followups.a: Each region has a different rule and no interleaving. Three simple loops are easier to prove correct than one loop with three-way branching.

learnings.insight: The obvious solution needs O(m+n) space for row and column flags. The O(1) solution notices that the first row and first column are themselves m+n cells that can serve as that flag storage - they just need special handling because they overlap at (0,0).
learnings.trick: Use one extra boolean for whether column 0 must be zeroed, since a[0][0] can only encode one of the two overlapping facts. Mark, then apply from the bottom-right backwards so markers are read before being overwritten.
edge_cases: The cell (0,0) is shared between the row-0 and column-0 markers - hence the extra flag.
Applying top-left first destroys markers before they are read; iterate in reverse.
A matrix that is already all zeros is handled naturally.

complexity.why: two passes over the matrix with a single extra boolean. The O(m+n) flag-array solution is the expected first answer; this is the follow-up.

followups.q: Why can't a[0][0] hold both markers?
followups.a: It sits in both row 0 and column 0, so zeroing it would be ambiguous. One extra variable breaks the tie.

followups.q: Game of Life with the same constraint.
followups.a: Encode both old and new state in one integer using two bits, then shift at the end. The same idea - reuse existing storage rather than allocating.

learnings.insight: Counting occurrences and rewriting is two passes and is perfectly correct. The problem wants one pass, which forces three-way partitioning - and Dutch National Flag is the canonical answer.
learnings.trick: Three pointers. low marks the end of the 0s, high the start of the 2s, mid scans. On a 0, swap with low and advance both. On a 1, just advance mid. On a 2, swap with high and DECREMENT high WITHOUT advancing mid.
edge_cases: mid must not advance after the 2-swap, because the value swapped in from high is unexamined. This is the single bug everyone writes.
The loop condition is mid <= high, not mid < high.
Already-sorted input does no swaps.

complexity.why: each element is examined once and mid never retreats, so the pass is linear. Counting sort is also O(n) but requires two passes.

followups.q: Generalise to k colours.
followups.a: Dutch National Flag only handles three. For k, counting sort is O(n + k) in two passes; one-pass k-way partitioning is not possible in O(1) space.

followups.q: Prove the invariant.
followups.a: [0, low) is all 0s, [low, mid) is all 1s, (high, n) is all 2s, and [mid, high] is unexamined. Every branch preserves this, and the loop ends when the unexamined region is empty.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II

tuf.striver_title: Best time to buy and sell stock II

learnings.insight: With unlimited transactions, any profitable multi-day hold decomposes into a sequence of profitable single-day holds, and any unprofitable day can simply be skipped. So the answer is the sum of every positive daily difference.
learnings.trick: Sum max(0, p[i] - p[i-1]). No state machine, no DP - just one pass. The decomposition argument is what makes the greedy exact rather than approximate.
edge_cases: Monotonically decreasing prices yield 0.
Buying and selling on the same day contributes nothing, which is why max(0, ...) is safe.
No transaction-count limit is what permits this; add one and greedy breaks immediately.

complexity.why: single pass with an accumulator. The DP formulation gives the same answer in O(n) but with two states - unnecessary here, essential once a limit appears.

followups.q: Add a transaction fee.
followups.a: Greedy breaks - you can no longer treat each day independently, because the fee makes short holds unprofitable. Switch to the two-state DP (holding / not holding).

followups.q: At most two transactions.
followups.a: LC 123. Track four states: after first buy, first sell, second buy, second sell. The generalisation to k is LC 188.

followups.q: Prove the decomposition.
followups.a: A hold from day i to day j yields p[j] - p[i], which telescopes to the sum of consecutive differences. Dropping the negative terms can only increase the total.

tuf.striver_title: Longest Consecutive Sequence in an Array

learnings.insight: Sorting gives O(n log n) and is the obvious answer. The O(n) solution needs one observation: only start counting a run from a value that has no predecessor in the set. That makes the apparently nested loop linear overall.
learnings.trick: Put everything in a hash set. For each x, skip unless x-1 is absent. When it is absent, x is a sequence head, so walk forward counting while x+1, x+2 ... exist.
edge_cases: Duplicates must not inflate the count - the set removes them automatically.
Empty input returns 0.
Negative numbers are fine; nothing here assumes positivity.

complexity.why: each value is visited at most twice overall - once as a head candidate and once inside exactly one run - so the inner while contributes O(n) in total, not O(n) per element.

followups.q: Why is the nested loop not O(n²)?
followups.a: The inner walk only runs for sequence heads, and each element belongs to exactly one sequence. So across all heads the inner loop performs n steps in total.

followups.q: Do it in O(1) extra space.
followups.a: Sort in place and scan adjacent elements, skipping duplicates. O(n log n) time but no extra memory - the standard trade.

followups.q: Union-Find alternative.
followups.a: Union each value with x+1 when present, then take the largest component. Same bound, more machinery, but it generalises to streaming insertions.

tuf.striver_title: Maximum Product Subarray in an Array

learnings.insight: Kadane's fails here because a negative number is not simply bad - multiplying by it turns the smallest running product into the largest. So you must carry both extremes forward, not just the maximum.
learnings.trick: Track curMax and curMin together. On a negative value, swap them before updating, because multiplication flips their roles. Each is then max/min of (x, curMax*x, curMin*x).
edge_cases: Zeros reset both running products to the element itself, which the max(x, ...) form handles without a special case.
A single negative element is the answer when it is the only element.
Overflow - products of 32-bit values need long long, or the constraints must bound it.

complexity.why: one pass with three scalars. The O(n^2) all-subarrays version is what this replaces.

followups.q: Why does tracking only the maximum fail?
followups.a: Because the optimal product ending at i may come from the most negative product ending at i-1 multiplied by a negative a[i]. Discarding the minimum discards that route.

followups.q: Prefix-product alternative.
followups.a: Scan left to right and right to left taking running products, resetting on zeros, and take the overall maximum. It works because a subarray with an even number of negatives is always bounded by one end or the other.

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

tuf.striver_title: Find minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

learnings.insight: The minimum is the single point where the descending step occurs. Comparing the midpoint against the RIGHT endpoint tells you which half contains that break - comparing against the left endpoint does not work reliably.
learnings.trick: While l < r: if a[m] > a[r] the break is right of m, so l = m + 1; otherwise the minimum is at m or left of it, so r = m. Never m - 1, or you can skip the answer.
edge_cases: An unrotated array returns a[0], which the a[m] <= a[r] branch handles.
Two elements is the tightest case - check it by hand.
With duplicates this degrades to O(n), which is LC 154.

complexity.why: each iteration halves the range. Note this cannot be O(log n) with duplicates, because a[l] == a[m] == a[r] carries no information.

followups.q: Why compare against a[r] and not a[l]?
followups.a: In an unrotated array a[m] > a[l] holds for the left half too, so the left comparison cannot distinguish rotated from unrotated. The right comparison can.

followups.q: How many times was the array rotated?
followups.a: The index of the minimum is exactly the rotation count - same algorithm, return the index.

followups.q: With duplicates.
followups.a: When a[m] == a[r] you cannot tell which side holds the break, so decrement r by one and accept O(n) worst case.

learnings.insight: Rotating by k is the same as reversing the whole array and then un-reversing the two pieces. Three reversals, no extra memory - and the derivation is more valuable than the trick itself.
learnings.trick: k %= n first, always. Then reverse(0, n-1), reverse(0, k-1), reverse(k, n-1).
edge_cases: k larger than n - without k %= n you reverse ranges out of bounds.
k = 0 or k = n is a no-op after the modulo.
The modulo must come before any use of k, including in the first reverse.

complexity.why: three linear reversals, each touching every element once. Using a temporary array is O(n) time but O(n) space, which the follow-up forbids.

followups.q: The cyclic-replacement alternative.
followups.a: Move each element directly to its destination, following cycles. The number of cycles is gcd(n, k), so you need an outer loop over starting points. One pass, but much easier to get wrong.

followups.q: Rotate left instead of right.
followups.a: Left rotation by k is right rotation by n - k. One line of adjustment.

learnings.insight: At most two values can each appear more than n/3 times, because three such values would need more than n elements. That bound is what makes a constant-space solution possible at all - you only ever need two candidates.
learnings.trick: Run two independent Boyer-Moore counters. The order of the branches matters: check 'matches candidate 1', then 'matches candidate 2', then 'counter 1 is zero', then 'counter 2 is zero', then decrement both. A verification pass at the end is mandatory.
edge_cases: The verification pass is NOT optional here - unlike n/2, existence is not guaranteed.
The two candidates must be initialised to distinct sentinel values, or an early element fills both slots.
Strictly more than n/3, so exactly n/3 does not qualify.

complexity.why: two passes, four scalars. A hash map solution is also O(n) time but O(n) space, which the follow-up rules out.

followups.q: Generalise to more than n/k times.
followups.a: At most k-1 such values exist, so keep k-1 candidates and counters. The verification pass stays mandatory. This is the Misra-Gries algorithm.

followups.q: Why must the branch order be exactly that?
followups.a: If you check for a zero counter before checking equality with the other candidate, a value equal to candidate 2 can overwrite candidate 1 when counter 1 happens to be zero, losing a genuine majority.

learnings.insight: Minimum removals equals n minus the maximum number of intervals you can keep, so this is classic interval scheduling inverted. Scheduling means sorting by END - keeping the earliest-finishing interval always leaves the most room.
learnings.trick: Sort by end. Keep a running `lastEnd`; take an interval when its start is at least lastEnd, otherwise count it as removed. Do not update lastEnd on a removal.
edge_cases: Touching intervals [1,2] and [2,3] do not overlap, so use >= not >.
Empty or single interval returns 0.
Sorting by start gives a wrong answer here - a long early interval blocks everything.

complexity.why: the sort dominates; the sweep is linear. The DP alternative - longest chain by compatibility - is O(n^2) and unnecessary.

followups.q: Prove sorting by end is optimal.
followups.a: Exchange argument: let G be greedy and O optimal, differing first at index i. Greedy chose the earliest-ending compatible interval, so end(G[i]) <= end(O[i]). Swapping G[i] into O keeps it valid and the same size, so greedy is optimal.

followups.q: Minimum arrows to burst balloons.
followups.a: Identical algorithm - count the intervals you keep rather than those you remove. LC 452.

followups.q: Intervals have weights and you want maximum total weight.
followups.a: Greedy fails. Sort by end and use DP with binary search for the latest compatible predecessor - O(n log n). That is LC 1235.

learnings.insight: Negative values are present in the constraints, which immediately rules out a sliding window - extending the window can decrease the sum, so shrinking is not a valid correction. Prefix sums with a hash map is the technique that survives negatives.
learnings.trick: A subarray (j, i] sums to k exactly when P(j) = P(i) - k. Keep a map from prefix value to how many times it has occurred, seeded with {0: 1} for the empty prefix, and add the lookup result to the answer at each step.
edge_cases: Seeding the map with {0, 1} is mandatory - without it every subarray starting at index 0 is missed.
Prefix sums overflow int at 1e5 values of 1e9 - use long long.
Count occurrences, not just presence; the same prefix value can recur many times.

complexity.why: one pass with O(1) average map operations. The O(n^2) nested-loop version is the brute force. Space is the map holding up to n distinct prefixes.

followups.q: Why not a sliding window?
followups.a: Sliding windows need monotone contributions. With negatives, adding an element can lower the sum, so the shrink rule is unsound and windows miss valid answers.

followups.q: Count subarrays with sum divisible by k.
followups.a: Same structure keyed on prefix sum mod k, with care to normalise negative remainders by adding k before taking the modulus.

followups.q: Longest such subarray rather than the count.
followups.a: Store the FIRST index at which each prefix value occurred, not a count, and take i - j.

learnings.insight: Reframe 'flip at most k zeros' as 'longest window containing at most k zeros'. That removes the flipping entirely and turns it into a standard variable-size window with a single counter.
learnings.trick: Expand right always, incrementing a zero counter. While the counter exceeds k, advance left, decrementing when the departing element is a zero. The answer is the largest window seen.
edge_cases: k = 0 degrades correctly to the plain longest-run problem.
All zeros with k >= n returns n.
The window is never shrunk below validity, so the answer is taken after the shrink loop.

complexity.why: each index enters and leaves the window exactly once, so the nested while contributes O(n) in total. One counter, no map needed since there are only two symbols.

followups.q: You must delete exactly one element.
followups.a: LC 1493 - same window with k = 1, then subtract one because the deletion is compulsory.

followups.q: The non-shrinking window variant.
followups.a: Some implementations never shrink, only slide, keeping the window at its maximum size. It works because the answer only needs the largest window ever achieved, and it removes the inner loop entirely.

learnings.insight: Counting subarrays with EXACTLY k odd numbers is awkward directly, but atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) gives it immediately - and atMost is a routine sliding window. This decomposition is worth more than the problem.
learnings.trick: Write a helper counting subarrays with at most k odd numbers by accumulating (r - l + 1) at each right endpoint, then return atMost(k) - atMost(k-1).
edge_cases: k = 0 must be handled - atMost(-1) is 0 by definition, so guard the helper.
Accumulating r - l + 1 counts every valid subarray ending at r, not just the longest.
The prefix-sum-on-odd-counts alternative also works and is worth knowing.

complexity.why: two linear passes, each a single window. The prefix-count map alternative is also O(n) but uses O(n) space.

followups.q: Solve it with prefix sums instead.
followups.a: Map the array to 1 for odd and 0 for even, then it is exactly Subarray Sum Equals K. Same problem in different clothing - noticing that is the real lesson.

followups.q: Why does atMost(k) - atMost(k-1) give exactly k?
followups.a: Every subarray with at most k is counted in the first term; those with at most k-1 are counted in both and cancel. What remains has exactly k.

learnings.insight: Every other binary search problem is a variation on this loop, so write it once, correctly, and never think about the boilerplate again. The two things that matter are the overflow-safe midpoint and picking one interval convention and keeping it.
learnings.trick: m = l + (r - l) / 2, never (l + r) / 2. Use closed [l, r] with `while (l <= r)` for exact match, and half-open [l, r) with `while (l < r)` for boundary searches.
edge_cases: (l + r) overflows int when both are near INT_MAX - this shipped broken in Java for nine years.
Single element and empty array must both terminate.
Mixing the two interval conventions is how infinite loops happen.

complexity.why: the range halves every iteration, so log2(n) iterations. Iterative form uses no stack.

followups.q: Write lower_bound and upper_bound.
followups.a: Half-open, r = n. lower_bound uses >=, upper_bound uses >. Count of x is the difference, which also gives first and last occurrence.

followups.q: Binary search on a linked list?
followups.a: O(n) to reach each midpoint makes it O(n log n) - worse than a linear scan. Random access is part of the precondition, not an incidental convenience.

learnings.insight: At index i the count of missing positives below a[i] is a[i] - (i + 1). That expression is monotonically non-decreasing, which is exactly the precondition binary search needs - so a linear scan becomes logarithmic.
learnings.trick: Binary search for the first index where a[i] - (i + 1) >= k. The answer is then l + k, where l is that index. Deriving that final formula on paper beats memorising it.
edge_cases: The answer may exceed every array element, which l + k handles without a special case.
k missing before the first element - the search returns l = 0 and the formula still works.
The array is strictly increasing by constraint, which is what makes the count monotone.

complexity.why: one binary search over the index space. The linear scan is O(n) and is the expected first answer before the follow-up.

followups.q: Derive the final formula.
followups.a: After the search, l elements are present below the answer, so the answer is the kth missing counted from 1 with l present numbers interleaved: l + k.

followups.q: The array is not sorted.
followups.a: Binary search is unavailable. Use a hash set and scan upward, or sort first at O(n log n).

learnings.insight: A rotated sorted array has exactly one break point, so for any midpoint, at least one half is still perfectly sorted. Identify which, then decide whether the target lies inside that sorted half - if it does, search there, otherwise search the other.
learnings.trick: Compare a[l] with a[m] to identify the sorted half. Then use a RANGE test on that half, not a single comparison: `a[l] <= target && target < a[m]`.
edge_cases: Use <= when comparing a[l] and a[m], or a two-element range misidentifies the sorted half.
The range test must be half-open on the correct side to avoid re-testing a[m].
With duplicates the identification fails and the worst case becomes O(n) - LC 81.

complexity.why: one half is discarded per iteration, exactly as in plain binary search. Finding the pivot first and then searching is two passes of O(log n) - same bound, more code.

followups.q: With duplicates.
followups.a: When a[l] == a[m] == a[r] neither half is identifiable - consider [1,1,1,0,1]. Shrink both ends by one and accept O(n) worst case. It is provably unavoidable.

followups.q: Find the pivot first, then search.
followups.a: Locate the minimum with one binary search, then run a standard search on the correct segment. Two O(log n) passes - easier to reason about, slightly more code.

problems.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array

learnings.insight: Do not find the element and then expand outward - with all-equal input that is O(n). Run two independent boundary searches instead, one for the first index >= target and one for the first index > target.
learnings.trick: first = lowerBound(target). If first == n or a[first] != target, return {-1,-1}. Otherwise last = upperBound(target) - 1. Two calls to the same half-open template.
edge_cases: Target absent entirely - the lower bound check catches it before the upper bound runs.
All elements equal to the target returns {0, n-1}, and is the case that kills the expand-outward approach.
Target larger than everything makes lowerBound return n; test that before indexing.

complexity.why: two independent binary searches, each halving the range. The expand-from-a-hit approach is O(log n + k) where k is the number of occurrences, which is O(n) in the worst case.

followups.q: Count occurrences without finding the positions.
followups.a: upperBound(x) - lowerBound(x) directly. Same two searches, no index handling.

followups.q: Why not find any occurrence and expand?
followups.a: With an array of identical values, expansion visits every element, making it O(n). Two boundary searches stay logarithmic regardless.

learnings.insight: When each row begins after the previous row ends, the matrix is already one sorted sequence. The only work is the index arithmetic that maps a flat position back to a row and column.
learnings.trick: Treat indices 0 to m*n-1 as one array and read g[mid / n][mid % n]. Division gives the row, modulo gives the column.
edge_cases: Use n (the column count) in both the division and the modulo - using m is the standard slip.
m*n can overflow int for very large matrices; the constraints here keep it safe.
Empty matrix or empty first row must be rejected before computing n.

complexity.why: one binary search over m*n candidates. Searching for the row first and then within it is O(log m + log n), which is the same bound.

followups.q: Rows are sorted but do not chain across rows.
followups.a: The flattening breaks. Use the staircase walk from the top-right corner, O(m + n) - that is LC 240.

followups.q: Two separate binary searches instead.
followups.a: Binary search the first column to find the candidate row, then search within it. Same complexity, and arguably clearer than the index arithmetic.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II

learnings.insight: The point of this problem is that duplicates break the O(log n) guarantee, and knowing WHY is more valuable than the code. When a[l] == a[m] == a[r] the array carries no information about which side holds the break.
learnings.trick: Add one branch to the LC 33 solution: when a[l] == a[m] && a[m] == a[r], do l++ and r-- and continue. Everything else is unchanged.
edge_cases: [1,1,1,0,1] is the canonical case that defeats naive half-identification.
Shrinking by one on each side is the only safe move - you cannot discard a half.
Worst case is O(n) and this must be stated, not hidden.

complexity.why: the ambiguous case degrades to linear scanning. An adversary can make every element equal except the target, forcing n comparisons - the bound is provably unavoidable.

followups.q: Prove O(n) is unavoidable.
followups.a: Given [1,1,...,1] with one element changed, any algorithm examining fewer than n elements can be defeated by an adversary placing the different value at an unexamined index.

followups.q: Does the same degradation hit Find Minimum with duplicates?
followups.a: Yes - LC 154, same reason and same fix.

learnings.insight: Binary search on an unsorted array looks impossible, but the invariant is not order - it is that the current range always CONTAINS a peak. If a[m] < a[m+1] the sequence is rising, so it must eventually fall or hit the boundary, and either way a peak lies to the right.
learnings.trick: Compare a[m] with a[m+1]. Rising means l = m + 1, falling means r = m. Half-open, so the loop cannot skip the answer.
edge_cases: The convention a[-1] = a[n] = -infinity is what makes boundary elements valid peaks.
Adjacent elements are guaranteed unequal by the constraints - without that the argument fails.
Any peak is acceptable, not the global maximum.

complexity.why: half the range is discarded each step even though the array has no global order, because the containment invariant is preserved by both branches.

followups.q: Justify discarding a half on unsorted data.
followups.a: If a[m] < a[m+1], the subarray [m+1, n) starts on a rise. It either keeps rising to the boundary - a peak by the infinity convention - or falls somewhere, producing a peak. So a peak is guaranteed in that half.

followups.q: 2D version.
followups.a: LC 1901. Binary search on columns; in each candidate column take the row-wise maximum and compare against its horizontal neighbours. O(m log n).

followups.q: What if adjacent elements may be equal?
followups.a: The comparison no longer determines a direction and the guarantee collapses - it becomes O(n) in the worst case.

learnings.insight: Rows and columns are individually sorted but the matrix is not globally sorted, so flattening fails. Starting at a corner where one direction increases and the other decreases turns each comparison into the elimination of an entire row or column.
learnings.trick: Start at the top-right. Larger than the target means the whole column is too big, so go left. Smaller means the whole row is too small, so go down. Bottom-left works equally well; the other two corners do not.
edge_cases: Top-left and bottom-right are useless starting points - both neighbours move the same direction, so no elimination is possible.
Loop bounds must allow i to reach m and j to fall below 0.
Empty matrix must be rejected first.

complexity.why: each step removes one full row or column, and there are m + n of them. Binary searching every row is O(m log n), which is worse whenever n is not much larger than m.

followups.q: Why not binary search each row?
followups.a: O(m log n) versus O(m + n). The staircase wins unless the matrix is extremely wide.

followups.q: kth smallest in such a matrix.
followups.a: Binary search on the VALUE range, counting elements <= mid with a staircase walk in O(m + n) per check. Total O((m+n) log(range)) - LC 378.

problems.title: Single Element in a Sorted Array

tuf.striver_title: Single element in a Sorted Array

learnings.insight: Before the unique element, every pair starts at an even index. After it, every pair starts at an odd index. That parity flip is a monotone predicate, which is exactly what binary search needs - the sortedness is almost incidental.
learnings.trick: Force m to be even with `m -= m & 1`. If a[m] == a[m+1] the unique element is to the right, so l = m + 2; otherwise r = m. The pairing is what you binary search on.
edge_cases: m must be even before the comparison, or the pairing logic inverts.
l = m + 2, not m + 1 - you are skipping a complete pair.
Single-element array returns it immediately.

complexity.why: each step discards half the pairs. XOR-ing the whole array is O(n) and also O(1) space, so the log bound is the only reason to prefer this.

followups.q: Why not just XOR everything?
followups.a: That is O(n). The array being sorted is the extra information that permits O(log n), and ignoring it is the mistake the problem is testing for.

followups.q: The index-XOR trick.
followups.a: `m ^ 1` gives m's pair partner regardless of m's parity - a neater way to express the same comparison without forcing evenness.

learnings.insight: The array is not what you search. The ANSWER - eating speed - is what has a monotone property: any speed that works means every faster speed also works. Recognising 'minimum X such that a condition holds' as the signature of answer-space search is the lesson.
learnings.trick: Binary search speed in [1, max(piles)]. feasible(k) computes total hours as the sum of ceil(p / k) and tests it against h. Use (p + k - 1) / k for the ceiling, never floating point.
edge_cases: Hours summed across 1e4 piles of 1e9 overflow int - accumulate in long long.
lo = 1, not 0 - speed zero never finishes.
hi = max(piles) is always feasible when h >= n, which the constraints guarantee.
Integer ceiling division: (p + k - 1) / k. `ceil(p * 1.0 / k)` introduces float error.

complexity.why: log(max) iterations of the search, each running an O(n) feasibility check. The value range is 1e9, so about 30 iterations.

followups.q: How do you know feasibility is monotone?
followups.a: Eating faster never takes more hours, so once a speed suffices every larger speed does too. State this before writing the loop - it is the correctness argument.

followups.q: How do you choose lo and hi?
followups.a: lo must be at or below the answer, hi must be feasible. Here hi = max(piles) finishes in exactly n hours, which is within any valid h.

followups.q: Minimise the maximum rather than the total.
followups.a: Split Array Largest Sum - same template, feasibility becomes a greedy partition count.

problems.title: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days

tuf.striver_title: Capacity to Ship Packages Within D Days

learnings.insight: Identical in shape to Koko, with a greedy feasibility check instead of an arithmetic one. Seeing two superficially different problems collapse to the same template is the point of doing both.
learnings.trick: Search capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)]. feasible(cap) greedily fills days: add weights until the next would exceed cap, then start a new day. Count days and compare to d.
edge_cases: lo must be max(weights), not 1 - a capacity below the heaviest package can never ship it.
hi = sum(weights) ships everything in one day and is always feasible.
Package order is fixed, which is what makes the greedy fill correct.

complexity.why: about 30 iterations of an O(n) greedy check. The greedy is exact because packages cannot be reordered - each day simply takes as much as it can.

followups.q: Why is the greedy fill optimal?
followups.a: Leaving capacity unused on a day can never reduce the total number of days, since the packages are in fixed order and must be shipped contiguously.

followups.q: Packages may be reordered.
followups.a: The problem becomes bin packing, which is NP-hard. The fixed order is what keeps this tractable - noticing that is worth saying aloud.

problems.title: Find the Smallest Divisor Given a Threshold

learnings.insight: Third instance of the same template, and by now you should recognise it from the phrasing alone: 'smallest divisor such that the sum is at most threshold'. Larger divisors give smaller sums, so feasibility is monotone.
learnings.trick: Search divisor in [1, max(nums)]. feasible(d) sums ceil(a[i] / d) and compares to the threshold. Integer ceiling again: (a[i] + d - 1) / d.
edge_cases: lo = 1, since divisor zero is undefined.
hi = max(nums) makes every term 1, giving a sum of n, which the constraints guarantee is within the threshold.
Sums fit in int here, but checking the constraints is the habit.

complexity.why: logarithmic search over the value range with a linear feasibility check.

followups.q: Name the three parts of any answer-space search.
followups.a: The monotone predicate, the lower bound, and the upper bound. Getting the bounds wrong is the usual failure, not the loop.

followups.q: Maximise rather than minimise.
followups.a: Flip the predicate and the branch assignments. The template is otherwise unchanged.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets

tuf.striver_title: Minimum days to make M bouquets

learnings.insight: The feasibility check here is a run-length scan rather than arithmetic, which is the only thing distinguishing it from Koko. Waiting longer never reduces the number of bouquets you can make, so the predicate is monotone in days.
learnings.trick: Search days in [min(bloom), max(bloom)]. feasible(d) walks the array counting consecutive flowers with bloomDay <= d, converting each run of length k into k / group bouquets and resetting the run on any later-blooming flower.
edge_cases: If m * k > n, no arrangement can ever work - return -1 before searching.
Adjacency is required, so the run counter must reset, not merely pause.
m * k overflows int when both are large - use long long for that check.

complexity.why: logarithmic search with a linear run-length check.

followups.q: Why check m * k > n first?
followups.a: It is the only case where the answer does not exist, and detecting it up front keeps the search bounds valid.

followups.q: Flowers need not be adjacent.
followups.a: Then it is simply the m*k-th smallest bloom day - sort or use nth_element. The adjacency constraint is what forces the scan.

learnings.insight: The 1D containment invariant lifts to two dimensions if you binary search columns and collapse each candidate column to its maximum element. That maximum is already the largest in its column, so only its horizontal neighbours can beat it.
learnings.trick: Binary search on the column index. In the middle column find the row-wise maximum, then compare it against its left and right neighbours to decide which half of the columns to keep.
edge_cases: Taking the column maximum is essential - an arbitrary element gives no guarantee vertically.
Boundary columns count as peaks under the -infinity convention.
Neighbours are only the four orthogonal cells, not diagonals.

complexity.why: log n column halvings, each scanning a column of m elements. Scanning the whole matrix is O(m*n).

followups.q: Why the column maximum specifically?
followups.a: It dominates vertically by construction, so if it also beats both horizontal neighbours it is a peak. If not, a larger neighbour guarantees a peak exists on that side.

followups.q: Binary search rows instead.
followups.a: Symmetric, giving O(n log m). Choose whichever dimension is smaller to search.

learnings.insight: Do not merge. The median is defined by a PARTITION: choose i elements from A and j = (m+n+1)/2 - i from B so that everything on the left is at most everything on the right. Binary searching i finds that partition in logarithmic time.
learnings.trick: Binary search on the smaller array. The partition is correct when A[i-1] <= B[j] and B[j-1] <= A[i]. Use ±infinity sentinels when i or j hits a boundary, which removes every edge case.
edge_cases: Always search the SMALLER array, or j can fall outside B's range.
Use LLONG_MIN and LLONG_MAX sentinels rather than branching on i == 0 or i == m.
Odd total length takes max of the left side; even takes the mean of the two middles.
Either array may be empty.

complexity.why: binary search over the partition index of the smaller array. Merging is O(m+n) and is the answer the problem explicitly rules out.

followups.q: Kth element of two sorted arrays.
followups.a: Same partition with i + j = k instead of the half-length. The median is the special case k = (m+n+1)/2.

followups.q: Why search the smaller array?
followups.a: It bounds the complexity by log(min(m,n)), and it guarantees j stays within B's valid range, which is what makes the sentinel handling sound.

followups.q: Extend to k sorted arrays.
followups.a: The partition argument does not generalise cleanly. Use a min-heap k-way merge, or binary search on the value rather than the index.

learnings.insight: Minimising a maximum is the clearest possible signal for answer-space binary search. Feasibility - can the array be split into at most k parts with no part exceeding X - is monotone in X, and checking it is a single greedy pass.
learnings.trick: Search X in [max(nums), sum(nums)]. feasible(X) greedily accumulates until adding the next element would exceed X, then starts a new part. Compare the part count to k.
edge_cases: lo = max(nums) - any smaller cap cannot hold the largest single element.
hi = sum(nums) is one part and always feasible.
Sums overflow int at 1000 values of 1e6 - use long long.
Aggressive Cows and Book Allocation are the same problem with different words.

complexity.why: about 30-40 iterations of an O(n) greedy check. The interval DP alternative is O(n^2 * k), which is what this replaces.

followups.q: Why is the greedy feasibility check correct?
followups.a: Filling each part as full as possible never increases the part count, because deferring an element to a later part can only add parts, never remove them.

followups.q: Solve it with DP instead.
followups.a: dp[i][j] = minimum possible largest sum splitting the first i elements into j parts. O(n^2 * k) - correct, but far slower and worth naming as the contrast.

followups.q: Aggressive Cows is the maximin version.
followups.a: Maximise the minimum gap rather than minimise the maximum sum. Same template, flipped predicate - LC 1552.

learnings.insight: Roman numerals are additive except when a smaller symbol precedes a larger one, which signals subtraction. So one lookahead comparison replaces the entire table of special cases like IV, IX, XL.
learnings.trick: Walk left to right. If value(s[i]) < value(s[i+1]), subtract it; otherwise add it. Six subtractive pairs collapse into that single rule.
edge_cases: The last character has no successor - guard the lookahead or handle it after the loop.
Only I, X and C can be subtractive, but the general rule handles that automatically.
Input is guaranteed valid, so malformed numerals need no rejection.

complexity.why: one pass over at most 15 characters with a fixed-size lookup table.

followups.q: Integer to Roman.
followups.a: Greedy: a descending table of values including the subtractive pairs (900, 400, 90, 40, 9, 4), repeatedly taking the largest that fits.

followups.q: Validate a Roman numeral.
followups.a: Now the special cases matter - a regular expression, or explicit rules about repetition limits and which subtractions are legal.

learnings.insight: Scanning vertically - character position across all strings simultaneously - lets you stop at the first mismatch, which is usually far sooner than comparing strings pairwise.
learnings.trick: For position i, check that every string has that position and that every character matches the first string's. Return the prefix of that length on the first failure.
edge_cases: Empty input returns an empty string.
A string shorter than the prefix so far terminates the scan - check length before indexing.
A single string is entirely its own prefix.

complexity.time: O(S) where S is the total characters
complexity.why: in the worst case every character of every string is examined, but the early exit makes it much faster in practice. Sorting and comparing only the first and last is O(S log n).

followups.q: Sort-based alternative.
followups.a: Sort the array; the common prefix of the whole set equals that of the first and last strings. O(S log n) but only two strings compared.

followups.q: Many queries against a fixed dictionary.
followups.a: Build a trie and walk down while each node has exactly one child and is not a word end.

learnings.insight: Nesting means the most recently opened bracket must close first, which is precisely a stack's contract. Any problem describing nesting is a stack problem before you have read the second paragraph.
learnings.trick: Push openers. On a closer, fail if the stack is empty or the top does not match. After the loop, the stack MUST be empty - forgetting that check lets '(((' pass.
edge_cases: Unclosed brackets - caught only by the final emptiness test.
A closer arriving on an empty stack must fail, not be ignored.
Odd-length input can be rejected immediately as a micro-optimisation.

complexity.why: one pass, with the stack holding at most n openers. No cleverness reduces the space, since fully nested input genuinely requires remembering every opener.

followups.q: Only one bracket type.
followups.a: A counter suffices - increment on open, decrement on close, fail if it goes negative. O(1) space. Multiple types are what force the stack.

followups.q: Return the longest valid substring.
followups.a: LC 32 - a stack of INDICES, or a two-pass counter sweep from both directions. Genuinely harder than the validity check.

tuf.striver_title: Check if String is Palindrome or Not

learnings.insight: The palindrome check is trivial; the problem is really about careful character filtering. Doing the filtering inline with two pointers avoids building a cleaned copy and keeps the space constant.
learnings.trick: Pointers from both ends. Advance each past any non-alphanumeric character, then compare the lowercased values. Skip inside the outer loop, not in a preprocessing pass.
edge_cases: A string of only punctuation is a valid palindrome - the pointers cross immediately.
The skip loops need their own bounds checks or they run past the ends.
Digits count as alphanumeric and must be compared, not skipped.

complexity.why: each pointer moves monotonically inward, so together they traverse the string once. Building a filtered copy first is the same time but O(n) space.

followups.q: One deletion is allowed.
followups.a: LC 680 - on the first mismatch, try skipping the left character or the right, and check whether either remainder is a palindrome. O(n) still, because only one mismatch is ever explored.

followups.q: At most k deletions.
followups.a: Becomes DP - the longest palindromic subsequence of length at least n - k. No longer a two-pointer problem.

learnings.insight: A mapping is not enough - you need a BIJECTION. Checking only s-to-t accepts ('badc','baba'), because two source characters may map onto one target. Both directions must be verified.
learnings.trick: Two arrays of size 256 storing last-seen positions, or two maps checked together. On each character pair, verify that the existing mapping in each direction is consistent before recording it.
edge_cases: ('badc','baba') is the case that defeats one-directional checking.
Different lengths fail immediately.
The position-array trick uses i+1 as the stored value so that 0 means 'unseen'.

complexity.why: one pass with two fixed-size tables, so constant space for a bounded alphabet.

followups.q: Word Pattern.
followups.a: LC 290 - exactly the same bijection check with words as the second alphabet instead of characters.

followups.q: Why is one direction insufficient?
followups.a: It permits a many-to-one mapping. Isomorphism requires structure preservation in both directions, which is precisely a bijection.

learnings.insight: Every rotation of s appears as a substring of s+s. That single observation replaces a loop over all n rotations with one substring search.
learnings.trick: Check the lengths match, then test whether goal is a substring of s + s.
edge_cases: Unequal lengths must be rejected first, or the containment test gives a false positive for a shorter goal.
Empty strings are rotations of each other.
s + s contains every rotation exactly once, plus s itself twice.

complexity.time: O(n²) with naive find, O(n) with KMP
complexity.why: the doubled string is O(n) space; the search dominates the time. With KMP the whole thing is linear.

followups.q: Make it O(n).
followups.a: Use KMP for the substring search instead of the library find, which is naive O(n*m) in libstdc++.

followups.q: Why does s + s contain every rotation?
followups.a: Rotating by k gives s[k:] + s[:k], which appears in s+s starting at index k. So all n rotations are substrings of the doubled string.

learnings.insight: You do not need a stack at all, only its depth. A counter tracks nesting level, and the outermost brackets are exactly those at depth 0 going in and depth 1 coming out.
learnings.trick: Increment on open, decrement on close. Append the character only when the depth before an open is non-zero, or after a close leaves the depth non-zero.
edge_cases: Order matters: for an open, append before incrementing; for a close, decrement before appending.
The input is guaranteed valid, so the counter never goes negative.
Concatenating repeatedly into a string is O(n^2) - reserve capacity.

complexity.why: one pass with a single integer. A stack would also work but stores information you never read back.

followups.q: When is a counter enough and when do you need a stack?
followups.a: A counter suffices with exactly one bracket type. With several, you must remember WHICH bracket is open, and only a stack does that.

problems.title: Maximum Nesting Depth of the Parentheses

tuf.striver_title: Maximum Nesting Depth of the Parentheses

learnings.insight: Same counter as the previous problem, reporting the maximum rather than filtering. Solving these back to back is the point - it makes the shared idea impossible to miss.
learnings.trick: Increment on open and take the maximum immediately; decrement on close. Non-bracket characters are ignored entirely.
edge_cases: The maximum must be taken at the increment, not after the loop.
Digits and operators are present and irrelevant.
Valid input guaranteed, so no negative-depth check is needed.

complexity.why: single pass, two integers.

followups.q: Input may be invalid.
followups.a: Track whether the depth ever goes negative and whether it ends at zero. Both must hold.

tuf.striver_title: Largest Odd Number in a String

learnings.insight: A number is odd exactly when its last digit is odd, and a prefix is always at least as large as any shorter prefix. So scan from the right for the first odd digit and return everything up to it.
learnings.trick: Walk from the last index backwards; the first odd digit found ends the answer. Return substr(0, i+1), or empty if none exists.
edge_cases: No odd digit anywhere means an empty string, not '0'.
The whole string may be the answer when it already ends in an odd digit.
Leading zeros are permitted in the output by the problem statement.

complexity.why: one backwards pass. The value is arbitrarily large so it cannot be parsed into an integer - the string is the only representation available.

followups.q: Why must you scan from the right?
followups.a: Longer prefixes are always larger numerically, so the answer is the longest valid prefix. Finding it means locating the rightmost odd digit.

learnings.insight: The canonical sliding window. The window is valid while it holds no duplicate, and the corrective move on a duplicate is to advance the left edge past the previous occurrence - not by one, which would be O(n^2) in the worst case.
learnings.trick: Store last-seen index per character. On seeing a repeat inside the window, jump l = max(l, lastSeen[c] + 1). The max() is essential - a stale occurrence outside the window must not drag l backwards.
edge_cases: Without max(), 'abba' gives a wrong answer: the second 'a' pulls l back behind 'b'.
Empty string returns 0.
Use int last[128] for ASCII rather than a hash map - faster and O(1) space.

complexity.why: each index is visited once by each pointer and l never retreats. The O(n^2) all-substrings check is what this replaces.

followups.q: Why is the max() necessary?
followups.a: lastSeen may point to an occurrence already left behind. Without max, l jumps backwards, re-admitting characters that were correctly excluded.

followups.q: At most k distinct characters instead of zero repeats.
followups.a: A frequency map plus a shrink condition on map size. LC 340, the premium version, but Fruit Into Baskets is the free k = 2 case.

followups.q: Return the substring rather than its length.
followups.a: Record the left index whenever the best length improves.

learnings.insight: A palindrome is defined by its centre, and there are only 2n-1 centres - n characters and n-1 gaps between them. Expanding outward from each is O(n^2) time but O(1) space, which beats the O(n^2)-space DP.
learnings.trick: For each index, expand for the odd case (i, i) and the even case (i, i+1). Missing the even case silently finds only odd-length palindromes.
edge_cases: Even-length palindromes like 'abba' are found only by the (i, i+1) expansion.
Single character is a palindrome of length 1.
Track the start index and length rather than building substrings during expansion.

complexity.why: 2n-1 centres, each expanding at most n/2 steps. The DP solution is the same time but O(n^2) space; Manacher's is O(n) but rarely required.

followups.q: Do it in O(n).
followups.a: Manacher's algorithm reuses previously computed radii by mirroring around the current palindrome's centre. Knowing it exists and naming the bound is usually sufficient.

followups.q: Count all palindromic substrings instead.
followups.a: LC 647 - identical expansion, incrementing a counter at every successful step rather than tracking a maximum.

followups.q: Longest palindromic SUBSEQUENCE.
followups.a: Entirely different - it is the LCS of s and reverse(s), O(n^2) DP. Subsequences need not be contiguous.

learnings.insight: There is no algorithm here. This is a specification-following exercise, and it is asked precisely to see whether you enumerate the requirements before coding rather than patching failures one test at a time.
learnings.trick: Four ordered phases: skip leading whitespace, read at most one sign, consume digits, stop at the first non-digit. Check overflow BEFORE each multiply, exactly as in Reverse Integer.
edge_cases: '   -42' has leading spaces; '+-12' is invalid after the first sign; 'words123' yields 0.
Overflow must clamp to INT_MAX or INT_MIN, not wrap.
Whitespace is only skipped at the start; internal spaces terminate parsing.
The empty string and a lone sign both yield 0.

complexity.why: one pass with a handful of scalars. The difficulty is entirely in the case analysis.

followups.q: Detect overflow without a 64-bit type.
followups.a: Before res = res*10 + d, test res > INT_MAX/10, or res == INT_MAX/10 && d > 7. The 7 comes from INT_MAX's last digit.

followups.q: Why clamp instead of wrapping?
followups.a: The specification says so, and signed overflow is undefined behaviour in C++, so wrapping is not even reliably reproducible.

learnings.insight: Generating all 2^(2n) strings and filtering is wasteful. Enforcing validity DURING construction - never close more than you have opened - prunes every invalid branch before it is built, so every leaf reached is a valid answer.
learnings.trick: Two counters. Add '(' while open < n. Add ')' while close < open. The second condition is the entire validity invariant, expressed as a pruning rule.
edge_cases: The condition is close < open, not close < n - that is what forbids ')(' prefixes.
n = 0 returns a single empty string.
Recursion depth is exactly 2n, so the stack is shallow.

complexity.why: the number of valid strings is the nth Catalan number, which is asymptotically 4^n / (n^1.5 * sqrt(pi)). Every leaf is a valid answer, so no work is wasted.

followups.q: Why is the count Catalan?
followups.a: Valid bracket sequences are in bijection with balanced paths that never dip below zero, which is the standard Catalan interpretation.

followups.q: Generate them iteratively.
followups.a: Build up by n using the Catalan recurrence: every valid string of length 2n is '(' + A + ')' + B for valid A and B of smaller sizes.

followups.q: Why prune instead of filter?
followups.a: Filtering generates 2^(2n) candidates of which only Catalan(n) are valid - exponentially more work for the same output.

learnings.insight: Each term is the run-length encoding of the previous one. There is no closed form and no shortcut - the value is in writing a clean run-length encoder without off-by-one errors.
learnings.trick: For each term, walk the previous string counting consecutive equal characters, appending count then character. Reserve capacity, since the strings grow quickly.
edge_cases: The final run must be emitted after the loop ends, or the last group is dropped.
n = 1 returns '1' with no iteration.
Counts can exceed 9 in principle, though not for small n - the code should still append the number as a string.

complexity.time: O(n · L) where L is the final length
complexity.why: n iterations, each linear in the current string. Length grows by roughly a factor of 1.3 per term (Conway's constant).

followups.q: In-place run-length compression.
followups.a: LC 443 - read and write pointers over the same array, since the compressed form is never longer than the original.

followups.q: Why does the length grow by ~1.3 per step?
followups.a: Conway's constant, the largest root of a degree-71 polynomial. Worth knowing as trivia, never worth deriving in an interview.

tuf.striver_title: Reverse words in a given string / Palindrome Check

learnings.insight: Reversing the entire string puts the words in the right order but each word backwards. Reversing each word individually then fixes them - the same decomposition as rotating an array, and it generalises.
learnings.trick: Reverse the whole string, then walk it reversing each word in place while simultaneously compacting: skip extra spaces and write words back with exactly one separator.
edge_cases: Leading, trailing and repeated internal spaces must all collapse to single separators.
A string of only spaces returns empty.
In-place compaction needs a write pointer trailing the read pointer.

complexity.space: O(1) in C++ where the string is mutable
complexity.why: two passes - one full reversal and one word-wise pass that also compacts. Splitting into a vector of words and rejoining is simpler but O(n) extra space.

followups.q: Reverse the characters of each word but keep word order.
followups.a: LC 557 - just the second pass, without the full reversal.

followups.q: Why is this the same idea as rotating an array?
followups.a: Both use the identity reverse(reverse(A) + reverse(B)) = B + A. Rotation applies it once; this applies it per word.

learnings.insight: A window is valid when windowLength - maxFrequency <= k, because the characters that are not the most frequent are exactly the ones you must replace. The surprising part is that maxFrequency never needs to be decreased when the window shrinks.
learnings.trick: Track a frequency array and a running maxFreq that is only ever increased. Shrink while (r - l + 1) - maxFreq > k. A stale maxFreq can never cause an incorrect acceptance.
edge_cases: Not recomputing maxFreq on shrink is correct but counter-intuitive - be ready to justify it.
k = 0 degrades to the longest run of a single character.
Uppercase letters only, so int cnt[26] suffices.

complexity.why: one pass with a 26-slot counter. Recomputing maxFreq inside the shrink loop would be O(26n), still linear but unnecessary.

followups.q: Why is a stale maxFreq safe?
followups.a: The answer only improves when a larger maxFreq appears. A stale, too-large value can make the window seem valid for longer, but it can never produce a window longer than the best genuinely achievable one, because that would require a real maxFreq at least as large.

followups.q: Return the actual substring.
followups.a: Record the left index whenever the window length improves.

learnings.insight: Count, then order by count. The only real decision is whether to sort the distinct characters (O(k log k)) or bucket them by frequency (O(n)), and the bounded alphabet makes the choice obvious once you notice it.
learnings.trick: Count into a fixed array, then either sort the (char, count) pairs by count descending, or bucket by frequency and read from the highest bucket down.
edge_cases: Ties may be output in any order here - do not over-engineer stability.
Build the output with reserve() or repeated append is O(n^2).
Case-sensitive: 'A' and 'a' are distinct characters.

complexity.time: O(n + k log k), or O(n) with bucketing
complexity.why: counting is linear; sorting only the distinct characters is cheap since k is bounded. Bucket sort by frequency removes the log entirely because frequencies are bounded by n.

followups.q: Make it O(n).
followups.a: Bucket sort: frequencies lie in [1, n], so index an array of buckets by frequency and read downward. Same instinct as counting sort.

followups.q: Rearrange so no two adjacent characters are equal.
followups.a: LC 767 - greedy with a max-heap, placing the most frequent remaining character that differs from the last placed. Impossible when one character exceeds (n+1)/2.

problems.title: Minimum Add to Make Parentheses Valid

tuf.striver_title: Minimum number of bracket reversals to make an expression balanced

learnings.insight: With a single bracket type you never need a stack, only its size. One counter tracks unmatched openers and another counts closers that arrived with nothing to match.
learnings.trick: Walk the string. On '(' increment open. On ')' decrement open if positive, otherwise increment the needed-openers count. The answer is the sum of both at the end.
edge_cases: A ')' arriving on zero open brackets requires an inserted '(' - it is not simply ignored.
Leftover open brackets at the end each need a ')'.
The empty string needs 0.

complexity.why: one pass with two integers. A stack would store openers you never inspect individually.

followups.q: Return the corrected string rather than the count.
followups.a: LC 1249 - mark unmatched indices using a stack of positions, then build the string skipping them. Here the stack is genuinely needed, because you need to know WHERE.

followups.q: Validate with a wildcard '*' that can be either bracket or empty.
followups.a: LC 678 - track a RANGE of possible open counts, [lo, hi], rather than a single value.

learnings.insight: Three pointers and a strict order of operations. Every harder list problem - reverse in groups, palindrome check, reorder - contains this loop, so getting it automatic pays for itself many times over.
learnings.trick: Save next BEFORE rewiring, because cur->next is about to be destroyed. Then point cur at prev, and advance both. Return prev, not cur - cur ends at nullptr.
edge_cases: Empty list returns nullptr; the loop simply does not execute.
Single node returns itself.
Returning cur instead of prev is the classic slip - cur is null when the loop exits.

complexity.why: one pass rewiring each pointer once. The recursive version is also O(n) time but O(n) stack, which matters at 1e5 nodes.

followups.q: Write it recursively.
followups.a: Recurse to the end, then on the way back set head->next->next = head and head->next = nullptr. Elegant, but O(n) stack - say so.

followups.q: Reverse only positions m to n.
followups.a: LC 92 - use a dummy head, walk to m-1, then splice nodes to the front of the sublist one at a time. The dummy is what removes the m = 1 special case.

learnings.insight: On a straight path a faster runner simply disappears ahead. On a circular one they must eventually lap the slower runner. So meeting is equivalent to the existence of a cycle - and it needs no memory at all.
learnings.trick: slow advances one, fast advances two. Guard with `while (fast && fast->next)` because fast dereferences two links per step.
edge_cases: The guard must check both fast and fast->next, or you dereference null on even-length acyclic lists.
A single node pointing to itself is a cycle.
Empty list has no cycle.

complexity.why: fast closes the gap by one node per step inside the cycle, so they meet within cycle-length steps of slow entering it. A hash set of visited nodes is also O(n) time but O(n) space.

followups.q: Why must they meet rather than pass each other?
followups.a: Inside the cycle the gap shrinks by exactly one each step, so it reaches zero - it can never jump from one to minus one.

followups.q: Find the cycle's length.
followups.a: Hold one pointer at the meeting point and advance the other until they coincide again, counting steps.

followups.q: Find where the cycle begins.
followups.a: LC 142 - reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time.

tuf.striver_title: Find the starting point in LL

learnings.insight: After the pointers meet, resetting one to the head and advancing both at the same speed brings them together exactly at the cycle entry. The proof is short and interviewers ask for it, so learn it rather than the code.
learnings.trick: Detect the meeting as in LC 141, then set slow = head and advance both one step at a time until they are equal. That node is the entry.
edge_cases: The reset must happen at the meeting point, not after any further movement.
No cycle means returning nullptr - handle it before the second phase.
The entry may be the head itself, which the algorithm handles naturally.

complexity.why: two linear phases. The hash-set solution is simpler but O(n) space, and this problem exists specifically to rule it out.

followups.q: Prove the reset works.
followups.a: Let k be the tail length and c the cycle length. When slow enters the cycle it has walked k and fast has walked 2k, so fast is k into the cycle. They meet k mod c before the entry. A pointer from the head needs k steps to the entry; the meeting pointer needs k too, walking k mod c plus whole loops. They arrive together.

followups.q: Apply it to an array.
followups.a: LC 287: with values in [1,n] treat a[i] as a next-pointer. The duplicate is the cycle entry. That disguise is the single highest-leverage one in DSA.

learnings.insight: When fast has covered the whole list, slow has covered half of it. The only real decision is which middle you want for even lengths, and that is set by the loop condition - decide deliberately rather than by accident.
learnings.trick: `while (fast && fast->next)` lands slow on the SECOND middle. `while (fast->next && fast->next->next)` lands it on the first.
edge_cases: Even-length lists have two middles and different problems want different ones.
Single node returns itself.
Counting the length first and walking n/2 works too but needs two passes.

complexity.why: one pass, and slow travels exactly half the distance fast does.

followups.q: Delete the middle node.
followups.a: LC 2095 - you need the node BEFORE the middle, so keep a prev pointer or start fast one step ahead.

followups.q: Which middle does a palindrome check want?
followups.a: Either works, provided the reversal of the second half is consistent with the choice. Being explicit about it avoids an off-by-one.

tuf.striver_title: Check if LL is palindrome or not

learnings.insight: Copying values into an array makes this trivial but costs O(n) space. The O(1) solution composes two techniques you already have - find the middle with fast/slow, then reverse the second half in place and walk the two halves together.
learnings.trick: Find the middle, reverse from there, compare until the reversed half runs out, then reverse it back so the caller's list is unmodified.
edge_cases: Restoring the list afterwards is what separates a careful answer from a passing one.
Odd length leaves a middle node that belongs to neither half and is skipped.
Empty and single-node lists are palindromes.

complexity.why: three linear phases - find middle, reverse, compare. The array-copy solution is the same time but O(n) space.

followups.q: Did you restore the input?
followups.a: Say yes and point at the line. Mutating a caller's structure without restoring it is a genuine defect, not a stylistic quibble.

followups.q: Why compare until the reversed half ends rather than the first?
followups.a: The first half may be one node longer when the length is odd. Terminating on the shorter side skips the unpaired middle automatically.

tuf.striver_title: Find the intersection point of Y LL

learnings.insight: Walk pointer A through list A then list B, and pointer B through B then A. Both travel exactly lenA + lenB before stopping, so they arrive at the intersection at the same moment - or at nullptr together if there is none.
learnings.trick: `a = a ? a->next : headB; b = b ? b->next : headA;` until a == b. No length computation and no extra structure.
edge_cases: No intersection means both become nullptr simultaneously and the loop ends - so the null case is handled by the same code path.
The switch must happen on null, not on the last node, or the lists never align.
Intersection is by node identity, not by value.

complexity.why: each pointer traverses both lists once. The length-difference solution is the same bound but needs two extra passes to measure.

followups.q: Why does the switch equalise the distance?
followups.a: Each pointer covers lenA + lenB in total regardless of starting side, so after that many steps they are at the same offset from the end - which is where the shared tail begins.

followups.q: The length-difference alternative.
followups.a: Measure both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference, then walk together. More intuitive, three passes instead of one.

tuf.striver_title: Add two numbers in Linked List

learnings.insight: The digits are stored least-significant-first, which is exactly the order addition needs. A dummy head removes the special case of creating the first result node, and handling the carry after the loop removes the special case of a final carry.
learnings.trick: Loop while either list remains OR the carry is non-zero. Inside, sum the two values plus carry, append sum % 10, and set carry = sum / 10.
edge_cases: A final carry creates an extra node - 5 + 5 = [0,1]. Including `|| carry` in the loop condition handles it.
Lists of different lengths - treat a missing node as 0.
Empty lists - the dummy head means the result is correctly null-ish.

complexity.why: one pass over the longer list. No extra space beyond the result, which is unavoidable.

followups.q: Digits stored most-significant-first.
followups.a: LC 445 - either reverse both lists, add, and reverse the result, or push onto two stacks and build the answer from the front. The stack version avoids mutating the input.

followups.q: Why include `|| carry` in the loop condition?
followups.a: Otherwise a carry generated by the last pair of digits is dropped, and 5 + 5 returns [0] instead of [0,1].

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

tuf.striver_title: Remove Nth node from the back of the LL

learnings.insight: You cannot index backwards in a singly linked list, but you can open a fixed gap between two pointers and walk them together. When the leader hits the end, the follower is exactly n from it.
learnings.trick: Start BOTH pointers at a dummy head, advance fast by n, then advance both until fast->next is null. Slow now sits on the node BEFORE the target, which is what you need to unlink it.
edge_cases: Removing the head itself is why the dummy exists - without it, n == length is a special case.
Starting both at the dummy rather than the head is what makes slow land on the predecessor.
n is guaranteed valid, so no bounds check is needed.

complexity.why: one pass. The two-pass version measuring the length first is equally O(n) and arguably clearer - say which you chose and why.

followups.q: Do it in two passes.
followups.a: Measure the length, then walk length - n steps. Simpler to reason about; the one-pass version is what the follow-up asks for.

followups.q: Why start at the dummy rather than the head?
followups.a: It shifts slow back by one so it lands on the predecessor instead of the target, and it makes removing the head identical to removing anything else.

problems.title: Delete the Middle Node of a Linked List

tuf.striver_title: Delete the middle node in LL

learnings.insight: Finding the middle is routine; deleting it requires its predecessor, which a plain fast/slow walk does not give you. Offsetting fast by one step at the start solves it without a separate prev pointer.
learnings.trick: Start fast at head->next->next so that slow stops one short of the middle, then unlink with slow->next = slow->next->next.
edge_cases: A single node has no middle to keep - return nullptr.
Two nodes delete the second one.
Leaking the removed node matters in C++ - delete it if you own the memory.

complexity.why: one pass at half speed. Counting the length first is two passes for the same result.

followups.q: Which middle does the problem want?
followups.a: The n/2-th using 0-based indexing, which is the second middle for even lengths. Confirm this from the examples before coding, not after failing a test.

problems.title: Delete Node in a Linked List

tuf.striver_title: Deletion of the head of LL

learnings.insight: You are given only the node to delete, with no access to its predecessor, so you cannot unlink it. The trick is to stop thinking about deleting the node and instead overwrite it with its successor's value, then delete the successor.
learnings.trick: node->val = node->next->val; node->next = node->next->next. You have effectively deleted the node's identity rather than the node itself.
edge_cases: This fails on the tail, which is why the problem guarantees the node is not last.
The successor node leaks unless explicitly freed.
Other pointers held to the successor node become dangling.

complexity.why: constant work regardless of list length, because no traversal happens at all.

followups.q: Why can this not work for the tail?
followups.a: There is no successor to copy from, and you cannot reach the predecessor to null its pointer. A sentinel tail node is the usual workaround in real systems.

followups.q: What breaks if someone else holds a pointer to the next node?
followups.a: It now points at a node that has been logically removed. This is exactly why real APIs give you the predecessor or an iterator rather than the node.

tuf.striver_title: Segregate odd and even nodes in Linked List

learnings.insight: Build two separate chains as you walk - one of odd positions, one of even - and splice them at the end. Trying to rearrange in place with a single pointer is far harder and buys nothing.
learnings.trick: Keep odd and even heads. Advance with odd->next = even->next, then even->next = odd->next. Save evenHead at the start so you can attach it after the odd chain.
edge_cases: evenHead must be captured before any rewiring, or you lose the even chain entirely.
The loop guard is `even && even->next`.
Fewer than three nodes needs no work.

complexity.why: one pass, rewiring each pointer once. No nodes are allocated - only existing links change.

followups.q: Group by value parity instead of position.
followups.a: Same two-chain structure, different predicate. LC 86, Partition List, is the version keyed on a pivot value.

followups.q: Is the relative order preserved within each group?
followups.a: Yes, because each chain is built by appending in traversal order. That stability is often required and is worth pointing out.

learnings.insight: Merge sort is the right algorithm for a linked list specifically because it never needs random access, and because merging relinks nodes rather than copying them - giving O(1) auxiliary space beyond the recursion stack.
learnings.trick: Split with fast/slow, cutting the list by setting prev->next = nullptr. Recurse on both halves, then merge with a dummy head.
edge_cases: The split MUST sever the first half, or the recursion never terminates.
A single node or empty list is the base case.
Recursion depth is O(log n), which is safe; a bottom-up iterative merge gives true O(1) space.

complexity.why: log n levels of recursion with O(n) merging each. Quick sort on a list needs O(n) to find a pivot and partitions awkwardly, which is why it is not used here.

followups.q: Achieve genuine O(1) space.
followups.a: Bottom-up merge sort: merge sublists of size 1, then 2, then 4, iterating rather than recursing. No stack at all.

followups.q: Why not quick sort?
followups.a: Pivot selection is O(n) without random access, and partitioning a list requires rebuilding chains. Merge sort's split is O(n) but its merge is natural for linked structures.

learnings.insight: Rather than rotating repeatedly, close the list into a ring, then walk to the correct position and cut it open again. One traversal to measure, one to cut.
learnings.trick: Walk to the tail counting the length, connect tail->next = head to form a ring, then advance (length - k % length) steps from the head and break the link there.
edge_cases: k may exceed the length - take k % length before doing anything.
k % length == 0 means no rotation; the ring must still be broken correctly.
Empty or single-node lists return unchanged.

complexity.why: two passes, or one if you combine the counting with reaching the tail. Rotating one step at a time k times would be O(n*k).

followups.q: Rotate left instead of right.
followups.a: Left by k is right by length - k. The ring makes both trivial once it exists.

followups.q: Why form a ring at all?
followups.a: It removes the need to track a separate new-tail pointer while walking, and makes the cut a single assignment.

tuf.striver_title: Clone a LL with random and next pointer

learnings.insight: The obvious solution maps old nodes to new ones in a hash map, which is O(n) space. The O(1) solution interleaves the copies into the original list, so each node's copy is simply node->next - the list itself becomes the map.
learnings.trick: Three passes. First, insert each copy immediately after its original. Second, set copy->random = original->random->next. Third, unweave the two lists, restoring the original.
edge_cases: A null random pointer must not be dereferenced in pass two.
The original list must be restored in pass three, not just the copy extracted.
An empty list returns null before any pass runs.

complexity.why: three linear passes with no auxiliary structure. The hash-map version is one pass but O(n) space, and this problem exists to rule it out.

followups.q: Why does interleaving work as a map?
followups.a: Because copy(x) is always at x->next by construction, so looking up any original's copy is a single dereference - exactly what the hash map provided.

followups.q: Clone an arbitrary graph.
followups.a: LC 133 - interleaving does not generalise, so you do need a map from original to copy, built during a DFS or BFS.

learnings.insight: Every element is either in or out, independently. That gives 2^n subsets and a two-branch recursion whose shape you will reuse for every subsequence problem for the rest of your life.
learnings.trick: At index i, push a[i] and recurse, then pop and recurse without it. Alternatively iterate masks 0 to 2^n - 1 and read the bits - the bitmask form is shorter and worth knowing.
edge_cases: The empty subset is a valid answer and must be emitted.
Pass the current path by REFERENCE and undo, or every node copies it.
n <= 20 in the constraints is the signal that exponential is intended.

complexity.why: 2^n leaves, each costing O(n) to copy into the result. The recursion depth is n.

followups.q: Write the bitmask version.
