followups.a: for (mask = 0; mask < (1<<n); mask++) collect elements where mask has bit i set. Same complexity, no recursion, and it makes the 2^n structure explicit.

followups.q: With duplicates in the input.
followups.a: Sort first, then skip a[i] == a[i-1] among siblings using `if (i > start) continue`. The condition is i > start, not i > 0.

learnings.insight: Duplicates in the input produce duplicate subsets. Sorting groups equal values together so that skipping repeated SIBLINGS in the recursion tree removes duplicates without any set or post-filtering.
learnings.trick: Sort. In the loop from `start`, skip when `i > start && a[i] == a[i-1]`. The condition is i > start and not i > 0, because equal values are allowed along a path - just not as alternative choices at the same level.
edge_cases: `i > 0` instead of `i > start` wrongly discards subsets containing repeated values.
Without sorting, equal values are not adjacent and the skip fails.
The empty subset is still required.

complexity.why: the same bound as Subsets in the worst case of all-distinct input; duplicates only reduce the output size.

followups.q: Explain i > start precisely.
followups.a: At a given recursion level, choosing the second of two equal values produces exactly the subtree the first already produced. Along a path, however, both copies may legitimately be taken - so the skip must apply only to siblings.

followups.q: Count distinct subsets without generating them.
followups.a: Multiply (count of each distinct value + 1) together. Pure combinatorics, no recursion.

learnings.insight: Elements may be reused, so the recursive call passes `i` rather than `i + 1`. That one character is the entire difference between this problem and Combination Sum II, and seeing it explicitly is worth more than either solution.
learnings.trick: Sort the candidates so you can `break` as soon as a[i] > target. That prune is frequently the difference between accepting and timing out.
edge_cases: Passing i + 1 instead of i silently forbids reuse and produces the wrong answer.
Starting the loop at `start` rather than 0 is what prevents permuted duplicates.
All candidates are positive, which is what guarantees termination.

complexity.why: the branching factor is the candidate count and the depth is bounded by target divided by the smallest candidate. Sorting enables the break, which prunes heavily in practice.

followups.q: What if candidates could be negative?
followups.a: Termination is lost - you could add and subtract forever. The positivity constraint is doing real work here.

followups.q: Count the combinations rather than listing them.
followups.a: That is unbounded knapsack DP in O(n · target), vastly faster. LC 518 is the coin version. Reading 'count' versus 'return all' changes the entire approach.

learnings.insight: Each element may be used at most once, and the input contains duplicates. So you need both changes at once: `i + 1` in the recursive call to forbid reuse, and the sibling skip to suppress duplicate combinations.
learnings.trick: Sort. Loop from start, skip when `i > start && a[i] == a[i-1]`, recurse with `i + 1`, and break when a[i] > target.
edge_cases: Both the i + 1 and the sibling skip are required - omitting either gives wrong output.
Duplicates in the input are the entire difficulty; without them this is trivial.
The same value may appear twice in a combination if it appears twice in the input.

complexity.why: each element is taken or skipped once, giving at most 2^n paths, heavily pruned by the sorted break.

followups.q: Why does the same skip rule work here as in Subsets II?
followups.a: The structure is identical - both enumerate choices at each level, and equal siblings generate identical subtrees.

followups.q: Combination Sum III, with a fixed count.
followups.a: Add a depth parameter and require exactly k elements drawn from 1..9. Same skeleton, two termination conditions instead of one.

learnings.insight: Two constraints must be satisfied simultaneously - exactly k numbers and exactly sum n - so the base case is a conjunction. The bounded candidate set 1..9 makes the search tiny regardless.
learnings.trick: Recurse with both remaining count and remaining sum. Succeed only when both hit zero; prune whenever either goes negative or the remaining candidates cannot reach the target.
edge_cases: Checking only the sum, or only the count, accepts wrong answers.
Numbers are 1 to 9 and each is used at most once, so at most 9 levels.
k > 9 or n > 45 is impossible and can be rejected immediately.

complexity.why: the candidate set is fixed at nine values, so the search space is bounded by a constant regardless of n.

followups.q: Add a stronger prune.
followups.a: The k smallest remaining candidates give a minimum achievable sum, and the k largest a maximum. If n falls outside that window, return immediately.

followups.q: Why is this so much cheaper than Combination Sum?
followups.a: The candidate set is bounded by a constant and reuse is forbidden, so the tree has at most 2^9 nodes.

learnings.insight: At each position, try every element not yet used. The swap-based formulation achieves this without a separate used[] array by exchanging the candidate into the current position and restoring it afterwards.
learnings.trick: For index i, loop j from i to n-1, swap(a[i], a[j]), recurse on i+1, then swap back. The restoring swap is the backtrack and omitting it corrupts everything downstream.
edge_cases: The loop must start at i, not i + 1, or the element already in place is never used.
n! grows brutally - 10! is 3.6 million, 12! is half a billion.
With duplicates, the swap formulation cannot dedupe cleanly - use used[] and sorting.

complexity.why: n! leaves, each costing O(n) to copy. The swap version avoids the O(n) used-array bookkeeping per node.

followups.q: With duplicates.
followups.a: Sort and use a used[] array with the rule `if (used[i] || (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i-1] && !used[i-1])) continue;`. Swapping breaks the sorted order and makes the skip unsound.

followups.q: Generate the kth permutation directly.
followups.a: Factorial number system - divide k by (n-1)! to pick each successive element. O(n^2) with no enumeration at all.

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

tuf.striver_title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

learnings.insight: This is a Cartesian product across the digit positions, so the recursion has one level per digit and a branching factor equal to that digit's letter count. There is no pruning because every combination is valid.
learnings.trick: Index into a fixed mapping array and recurse one digit at a time, appending and then popping a character. Iterative BFS-style building works equally well.
edge_cases: Empty input returns an empty list, not a list containing an empty string.
Digits 7 and 9 have four letters, which affects the count but not the structure.
Digits 0 and 1 do not appear by constraint.

complexity.why: at most 4 letters per digit over n digits, with O(n) to copy each completed string.

followups.q: Build it iteratively.
followups.a: Start with a list containing the empty string and, for each digit, replace the list with every existing prefix extended by every letter. Clearer to some, same complexity.

followups.q: Why is there no pruning here?
followups.a: Every combination is valid by definition, so there is nothing to reject. Contrast with Generate Parentheses, where pruning eliminates exponentially many invalid branches.

learnings.insight: DFS from every cell, marking visited cells in place and restoring them on the way out. Marking in the grid itself rather than in a separate visited array keeps the space O(1) beyond recursion.
learnings.trick: Overwrite the cell with a sentinel such as '#' before recursing, and restore the original character afterwards. Check the character match before recursing, not after.
edge_cases: The restore on failure is mandatory - without it, later starting cells see a corrupted grid.
Bounds and character mismatch must both be checked before any recursion.
The same cell may not be reused within one path but may be reused across different starting points.

complexity.why: every cell is a potential start, and from each the search branches up to four ways for the word length L. In practice the character check prunes almost immediately.

followups.q: Search for many words at once.
followups.a: LC 212 - build a trie of the words and DFS the grid once against it, pruning whenever the current prefix leaves the trie. Vastly better than running this once per word.

followups.q: Why mark in place rather than use a visited array?
followups.a: It is O(1) extra space and one assignment. The only cost is mutating the input, which must be restored - and in a threaded context would be unsafe.

learnings.insight: Place one queen per row, so the only choice per level is the column. The real skill is making the validity test O(1) with three marker arrays instead of rescanning the board.
learnings.trick: Keep boolean arrays for columns, for the i+j diagonal, and for the i-j+n anti-diagonal. Every cell on a diagonal shares those sums, so conflict detection is three array reads.
edge_cases: The anti-diagonal index i-j can be negative - offset by n.
Restoring all three markers on backtrack is required.
n = 2 and n = 3 have no solutions; n = 1 has one.

complexity.why: the first row has n choices, the next at most n-1 and so on, but constraint pruning cuts the real tree far below n!. The O(1) validity check is what makes it fast in practice.

followups.q: Count solutions without building boards.
followups.a: LC 52 - drop the board entirely and return a count. Bitmask versions represent all three constraint sets in three integers and are dramatically faster.

followups.q: Why is placing one queen per row sufficient?
followups.a: Two queens in the same row always conflict, so any solution has exactly one per row. Encoding that structurally removes an entire constraint for free.

learnings.insight: Find an empty cell, try each digit that does not conflict, recurse, and undo on failure. The naive version rescans row, column and box for every candidate; the fast version maintains three constraint tables and checks in O(1).
learnings.trick: Maintain rowUsed[9][10], colUsed[9][10] and boxUsed[9][10], with the box index computed as (i/3)*3 + j/3. Return true immediately on success so the search stops.
edge_cases: Box index arithmetic (i/3)*3 + j/3 is the usual slip.
Returning true must propagate all the way up or the solved board is overwritten by further search.
All three tables must be cleared on backtrack.

complexity.time: O(9^m) where m is the number of blanks
complexity.why: each blank has at most nine candidates. Constraint propagation prunes so aggressively that real puzzles solve almost instantly despite the bound.

followups.q: Choose the most-constrained cell first.
followups.a: Instead of the first empty cell, pick the one with fewest legal candidates. This minimum-remaining-values heuristic cuts the tree dramatically.

followups.q: Use bitmasks for the constraint sets.
followups.a: One 9-bit integer per row, column and box. Candidate generation becomes a single AND, and iterating candidates uses x & -x.

learnings.insight: Repeated multiplication is O(n) and times out for n up to 2^31. Squaring the base and halving the exponent is O(log n), and the same identity underlies modular exponentiation everywhere in competitive programming.
learnings.trick: While n > 0: if n is odd multiply the result by the base, then square the base and halve n. Handle negative n by inverting the base and negating n - in long long, because -INT_MIN overflows.
edge_cases: n = INT_MIN cannot be negated in int - promote to long long before negating.
x = 0 with negative n is undefined; the constraints exclude it.
Floating-point error accumulates, so the expected answer has a tolerance.

complexity.why: the exponent halves each iteration, so about 31 iterations for a 32-bit exponent.

followups.q: Why does -INT_MIN overflow?
followups.a: Two's complement has one more negative value than positive, so INT_MIN has no positive counterpart. Promote to long long before negating.

followups.q: Modular exponentiation.
followups.a: Same loop with `% mod` after each multiply. This is how modular inverses are computed via Fermat's little theorem, and it is far more commonly needed than the float version.

learnings.insight: Assigning + or - to each number looks like pure enumeration at 2^n, but it is really a subset-sum problem: if P is the set given +, then sum(P) = (total + target) / 2. That reframing turns exponential search into a knapsack DP.
learnings.trick: Check that (total + target) is non-negative and even, then count subsets summing to half of it with a 1D DP iterated downward over the capacity.
edge_cases: (total + target) odd, or |target| > total, means zero ways - return before the DP.
Zeros in the array double the count for each, which the DP handles naturally but enumeration must not miss.
The capacity loop must run DOWNWARD for 0/1 usage.

complexity.why: the DP table has n items by sum capacities, rolled to one row. The brute force is O(2^n), which is 2^20 at the constraint limit - passable but far slower.

followups.q: Derive the transformation.
followups.a: Let P be the plus set and N the minus set. sum(P) - sum(N) = target and sum(P) + sum(N) = total, so sum(P) = (total + target) / 2.

followups.q: Why must the loop run downward?
followups.a: Upward would allow each number to be used more than once, which is the unbounded knapsack. Direction is the only difference between the two.

learnings.insight: Checking all 32 positions works and is O(32). Brian Kernighan's trick - `x &= x - 1` clears the lowest set bit - makes it O(popcount), which matters when most bits are zero.
learnings.trick: Loop `while (x) { x &= x - 1; count++; }`. Subtracting one flips the lowest set bit to zero and everything below it to one; the AND then clears exactly that bit.
edge_cases: Use unsigned, or a negative input right-shifts arithmetically and loops forever in the shift-based version.
x = 0 returns 0 without entering the loop.
__builtin_popcount compiles to a single instruction on supporting hardware.

complexity.why: each iteration removes exactly one set bit, so the loop runs popcount times rather than 32.

followups.q: Prove why x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit.
followups.a: x-1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and all trailing 0s into 1s, leaving higher bits unchanged. ANDing therefore clears that bit and preserves everything above it.

followups.q: Count set bits for every number from 0 to n.
followups.a: LC 338 - dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1), or dp[i] = dp[i & (i-1)] + 1. O(n) total rather than O(n log n).

learnings.insight: Counting each number independently is O(n log n). The DP observation is that i's bit count is i-without-its-lowest-bit plus one, or equivalently i-shifted-right plus its last bit - either gives O(n) total.
learnings.trick: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Right-shifting drops the last bit, whose value you add back directly. dp[i] = dp[i & (i-1)] + 1 is the equivalent Kernighan form.
edge_cases: dp[0] = 0 seeds the recurrence.
The result array has n+1 entries, not n.
Both recurrences read a strictly smaller index, so a single forward pass is valid.

complexity.why: one constant-time transition per number. Calling popcount n times is O(n log n) or O(n) with hardware support, but the DP is the intended answer.

followups.q: Derive both recurrences.
followups.a: i >> 1 removes the last bit, so add it back with i & 1. i & (i-1) removes the LOWEST SET bit, so add exactly one. Different decompositions, same result.

followups.q: Do it without any DP array.
followups.a: Not possible in O(n) - the output itself is the array. The DP is free given that the output must be materialised anyway.

learnings.insight: Shift out of the source and into the result 32 times. It is the same structure as reversing decimal digits, with base 2 instead of base 10 - which is the general lesson about digit extraction.
learnings.trick: res = (res << 1) | (n & 1), then n >>= 1, repeated exactly 32 times. Not while n is non-zero - leading zeros of the input are trailing bits of the output and must be shifted in.
edge_cases: Looping while n != 0 drops trailing zeros in the result - always loop exactly 32 times.
Use uint32_t; right-shifting a negative signed int is implementation-defined.
The follow-up about repeated calls is the real question.

complexity.why: a fixed 32 iterations regardless of input, so effectively constant.

followups.q: The function is called many times. Optimise it.
followups.a: Cache reversals of each byte in a 256-entry table, then reverse a 32-bit word with four lookups and three shifts. Classic space-for-time trade.

followups.q: Do it in O(log 32) with no loop.
followups.a: Divide-and-conquer bit swaps: swap adjacent bits, then pairs, then nibbles, then bytes, then halves. Five masked operations total.

tuf.striver_title: Check if a Number is Power of 2 or Not

learnings.insight: A power of two has exactly one set bit, so `x & (x - 1)` must be zero. The positivity guard is not optional - it is what excludes zero and negative numbers, which also satisfy the bit test.
learnings.trick: `return x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0;`. Both halves are load-bearing.
edge_cases: x = 0 passes the bit test but is not a power of two - hence x > 0.
Negative powers of two in two's complement also pass the bit test.
x = 1 is 2^0 and must return true.

complexity.why: two operations, no loop. The repeated-division approach is O(log n) and unnecessary.

followups.q: Power of four.
followups.a: Also a single set bit, but at an even position - add a mask test against 0x55555555. Alternatively (x - 1) % 3 == 0 for powers of two.

followups.q: Power of three without loops or recursion.
followups.a: 3^19 = 1162261467 is the largest power of three in an int, so test divisibility into it. The trick only works because 3 is prime.

learnings.insight: Bit tricks do not apply to non-binary bases, so the shortcut here is number-theoretic: since 3 is prime, every power of three divides the largest power of three that fits in an int, and nothing else does.
learnings.trick: 3^19 = 1162261467 is the largest power of three below INT_MAX, so return `n > 0 && 1162261467 % n == 0`.
edge_cases: n must be positive, or the modulo is meaningless.
This relies on 3 being prime; it would not work for base 4 or 6.
The loop-based version dividing by 3 repeatedly is perfectly acceptable and clearer.

complexity.why: a single modulo. The iterative division version is O(log n), which is also fine.

followups.q: Why does the divisibility trick require a prime base?
followups.a: The divisors of p^k for prime p are exactly p^0..p^k. For a composite base the divisors include products of its factors, so non-powers would pass.

followups.q: Why not log(n)/log(3) and check for an integer?
followups.a: Floating-point rounding makes it unreliable at the boundaries - it misclassifies some genuine powers.

problems.title: Minimum Bit Flips to Convert Number

tuf.striver_title: Minimum Bit Flips to Convert Number

learnings.insight: XOR sets a bit exactly where the two numbers differ, so the number of flips needed is simply the population count of the XOR. Two operations, no loop over positions.
learnings.trick: `return __builtin_popcount(start ^ goal);` - or Brian Kernighan's loop if built-ins are disallowed.
edge_cases: Identical inputs give XOR zero and therefore zero flips.
Works for any bit width; use popcountll for 64-bit.
Negative values work on the bit pattern, though the constraints here are positive.

complexity.why: one XOR and one population count, both constant-time on fixed-width integers.

followups.q: This is Hamming distance.
followups.a: LC 461 is literally the same problem under a different name. Recognising renamed problems quickly is worth practising.

followups.q: Total Hamming distance across all pairs in an array.
followups.a: LC 477 - for each bit position count how many numbers have it set, say k of n; that position contributes k * (n - k). O(32n) rather than O(n^2).

tuf.striver_title: Divide two numbers without multiplication and division

learnings.insight: Repeated subtraction is O(quotient) and times out. Doubling the divisor while it still fits - the same idea as binary exponentiation - makes it O(log n). The overflow cases are the real difficulty.
learnings.trick: Work in long long and in the negative domain, since INT_MIN has no positive counterpart. Shift the divisor left while it fits, subtract, and accumulate the corresponding power of two.
edge_cases: INT_MIN / -1 overflows and must be special-cased to INT_MAX.
abs(INT_MIN) is undefined behaviour - never call it.
Truncation is toward zero, so the sign must be applied after the magnitude is computed.
Divisor of 1 or -1 should be handled directly.

complexity.time: O(log² n) naive, O(log n) careful
complexity.why: each outer step at least halves the remaining dividend. Recomputing the shift from scratch each time gives the squared bound; carrying it forward avoids that.

followups.q: Why work in the negative domain?
followups.a: INT_MIN can be represented but its negation cannot. Negating both operands to negative means every intermediate value is representable.

followups.q: Which single input overflows the result?
followups.a: INT_MIN / -1 = 2147483648, one past INT_MAX. It is the only such case and must return INT_MAX by specification.

tuf.striver_title: Count primes in range L to R

learnings.insight: Testing each number for primality is O(n sqrt n). The sieve inverts the work - instead of asking whether each number is prime, it marks the multiples of each prime - giving O(n log log n), which is very nearly linear.
learnings.trick: Start the inner loop at i*i, not 2i: every smaller multiple of i has a factor below i and was already marked. Outer loop only while i*i <= n.
edge_cases: 0 and 1 are not prime and must be marked false explicitly.
i*i overflows int for large n - use long long in the loop bounds.
The answer counts primes strictly less than n, not up to and including it.

complexity.why: the inner loop runs n/p times per prime p, and the sum of 1/p over primes up to n is ln ln n by Mertens' theorem.

followups.q: Why start at i*i?
followups.a: Any multiple k*i with k < i has the smaller factor k, so it was crossed out when the sieve processed k. Starting earlier is correct but wasteful.

followups.q: Make it O(n).
followups.a: The linear sieve marks each composite exactly once by its smallest prime factor, and gives you that factor for free - which makes later factorisations O(log n).

followups.q: Halve the memory.
followups.a: Skip even numbers entirely and index only odds, or use a bitset instead of vector<bool> - though vector<bool> is already bit-packed in libstdc++.

problems.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

tuf.striver_title: Maximum XOR of two numbers in an array

learnings.insight: The O(n^2) pairwise scan is obvious. The insight that makes it O(32n) is that a trie can index BITS rather than characters - insert every number as a 32-bit path, then for each number walk greedily preferring the opposite bit at every level.
learnings.trick: Greedy works because a higher bit outweighs every lower bit combined: setting bit k gains 2^k, while all bits below sum to 2^k - 1. So take the opposite branch whenever it exists.
edge_cases: Insert all numbers before querying, or you miss pairs.
Fixed 32-bit depth regardless of the values.
Fall back to the same branch when the opposite child is absent.

complexity.why: each number is inserted and queried in 32 steps. The trie holds at most 32n nodes.

followups.q: Why is the greedy bit choice optimal?
followups.a: 2^k > 2^k - 1 = sum of all lower bits, so securing a higher bit always beats any combination of lower ones. Greedy from the top is therefore exact.

followups.q: Prefix-mask alternative without a trie.
followups.a: Build the answer bit by bit from the top, keeping a hash set of prefixes at each level and testing whether the desired complement exists. Same bound, no trie structure.

learnings.insight: getMin must be O(1), which rules out scanning. The fix is to remember, alongside every element, what the minimum was at the moment it was pushed - so popping automatically restores the previous minimum.
learnings.trick: Push min(x, currentMin) onto a second stack on every push, and pop both together. No conditional logic and no risk of losing a minimum.
edge_cases: Duplicate minimums must be pushed every time, or popping one loses the other.
getMin on an empty stack is undefined - the problem guarantees valid calls.
Pushing the min unconditionally is simpler and safer than pushing only on improvement.

complexity.why: every operation is a constant number of stack operations. The auxiliary stack doubles memory, which the O(1)-space variant avoids at the cost of overflow risk.

followups.q: Do it without the second stack.
followups.a: Store 2*x - min when a new minimum arrives, and recover the previous minimum on pop. It works but can overflow, so it is worth naming rather than implementing.

followups.q: A max stack with the same guarantees.
followups.a: Symmetric. A stack supporting both min and max needs two auxiliary stacks or one of pairs.

followups.q: popMax in O(log n).
followups.a: Requires an ordered structure alongside the stack - a multiset plus a doubly linked list. That is LC 716.

learnings.insight: One stack reverses order; two stacks reverse it twice, restoring FIFO. The transfer must happen only when the output stack is empty, which is what makes the amortised cost constant rather than linear.
learnings.trick: Push onto the input stack. On pop or peek, if output is empty, drain input into output entirely, then operate on output. Never transfer partially.
edge_cases: Transferring when output is non-empty destroys the ordering.
empty() must check both stacks.
A single pop can be O(n); only the amortised cost is O(1).

complexity.why: each element is pushed and popped at most twice across both stacks, so n operations cost O(n) in total. A single operation can still be O(n).

followups.q: Is pop worst-case O(1)?
followups.a: No - the transfer makes one pop O(n). Amortised O(1) is the honest claim, and the distinction is what the question is testing.

followups.q: Stack using queues.
followups.a: LC 225 - either make push O(n) by rotating the queue after each insert, or make pop O(n). You cannot have both at O(1) with queues.

learnings.insight: A queue gives FIFO, so producing LIFO requires moving the cost somewhere. Rotating the queue after each push puts the newest element at the front, making push O(n) and everything else O(1).
learnings.trick: Push, then dequeue and re-enqueue the preceding size-1 elements. One queue suffices; the two-queue version is no better.
edge_cases: Rotate size-1 times, not size times.
A single queue is enough - two is a common over-complication.
Unlike the queue-from-stacks case, the cost here is not amortisable away.

complexity.time: O(n) push, O(1) pop and top
complexity.why: the rotation touches every existing element on each push. The reverse trade - O(1) push and O(n) pop - is equally valid.

followups.q: Why can't this be O(1) amortised like the stack version?
followups.a: Stacks reverse order, so two reversals restore it and each element moves a bounded number of times. A queue preserves order, so every push must re-establish LIFO from scratch.

learnings.insight: This is the gateway to the entire monotonic stack family. Once an element has a smaller element to its right, that smaller one can never be anyone's answer - so it can be discarded permanently, which is what makes the pass linear.
learnings.trick: Walk nums2 keeping a decreasing stack. Anything the current value exceeds is popped, and the current value is its next greater. Record results in a map, then read off for nums1.
edge_cases: Elements left on the stack at the end have no greater element - default to -1.
nums1 is a subset of nums2, so a map lookup is needed rather than index alignment.
Values are distinct here, which removes tie handling.

complexity.why: each element is pushed and popped once, so the inner while contributes O(n) in total. The nested-loop version is O(n*m).

followups.q: Why is the inner while not making this quadratic?
followups.a: Each index enters the stack once and leaves once, so total pops across the whole run are bounded by n regardless of how many occur on any single step.

followups.q: Next SMALLER element.
followups.a: Flip the comparison and the stack becomes increasing. That one character switches the entire family.

learnings.insight: Circularity is handled by pretending the array is twice as long. Iterating 2n times with index i % n lets the wrap-around candidates be considered without physically duplicating anything.
learnings.trick: Loop i from 0 to 2n-1, using a[i % n]. Only record answers during the first pass, or during the second - but push indices throughout so wrapped candidates are available.
edge_cases: Only write results for indices below n, or the second pass overwrites correct answers.
Indices stored on the stack must be modulo n.
All-equal arrays leave every answer at -1, since 'greater' is strict.

complexity.why: 2n iterations with each index pushed and popped at most once, so still linear.

followups.q: Why 2n and not 3n?
followups.a: Every element can see all n-1 others within one full wrap, so two passes suffice. A third adds nothing.

followups.q: Circular subarray maximum sum.
followups.a: Different technique - either a normal Kadane, or total minus the minimum subarray. The doubling trick is not the universal answer to circularity.

learnings.insight: Identical to Next Greater Element, but the answer is a DISTANCE rather than a value - which is precisely why the stack must hold indices. This is the problem that teaches you never to store values in a monotonic stack.
learnings.trick: Decreasing stack of indices. When the current temperature exceeds the one at the stack top, the answer for that index is i - stackTop.
edge_cases: Store indices, not temperatures, or the distance is unrecoverable.
Indices never popped keep their default answer of 0.
Equal temperatures do not count as warmer - use strict comparison.

complexity.why: each index is pushed and popped once. The pairwise scan is O(n^2) and is what this replaces.

followups.q: Solve it right to left instead.
followups.a: Walk backwards with an increasing stack, popping anything not warmer. Equivalent, and some find the direction more intuitive.

followups.q: The temperature range is bounded at 30 to 100.
followups.a: That permits an O(n * 71) solution tracking the next occurrence of each temperature - worse in theory, but it shows you noticed the constraint.

learnings.insight: Spans compose: when you pop an element, you inherit its span rather than recounting. That inheritance is what keeps the amortised cost constant even though a single call may pop many entries.
learnings.trick: Stack of (price, span) pairs. While the top price is at most the new price, pop and add its span to the current one. Push the accumulated pair.
edge_cases: Prices equal to the current one count toward the span - use <=, not <.
The span includes today, so it starts at 1.
A monotonically decreasing price sequence gives every span as 1.

complexity.why: each price is pushed once and popped once across the lifetime of the object, so n calls cost O(n) in total.

followups.q: Why can you add the popped span instead of recounting?
followups.a: The popped element already spans a contiguous block of smaller-or-equal prices, and that entire block is also smaller than the current price by transitivity.

followups.q: Support removing the most recent price.
followups.a: Needs an undo log of what each push popped, so the stack can be restored - a persistent structure rather than a plain stack.

learnings.insight: Only a right-moving asteroid already on the stack can collide with an incoming left-moving one. Every other pairing is safe, and that single observation reduces the whole simulation to one stack pass.
learnings.trick: Push positives unconditionally. For a negative, loop while the top is positive and smaller in magnitude, popping. Then handle the three outcomes: equal magnitudes destroy both, a larger top survives and the incoming is destroyed, or the stack is clear and it is pushed.
edge_cases: Equal magnitudes destroy BOTH - pop the top and do not push the incoming.
Two negatives never collide, nor do two positives.
A negative arriving on an empty stack survives permanently.
The alive flag pattern is cleaner than deeply nested branches.

complexity.why: each asteroid is pushed and popped at most once. The naive repeated-scan simulation is O(n^2).

followups.q: Asteroids of equal size pass through instead of destroying each other.
followups.a: The equality branch becomes a no-op push rather than a mutual destruction - a one-line change, which is the point of isolating the three cases.

followups.q: Why can two negatives never collide?
followups.a: They move in the same direction at the same speed, so the gap between them is constant.

learnings.insight: To make a number as small as possible, remove a digit whenever it is followed by a smaller one - that swap lowers a more significant place. A monotonic increasing stack performs exactly those removals greedily.
learnings.trick: Maintain an increasing stack, popping while the top exceeds the incoming digit and removals remain. If k is still positive at the end, drop from the back. Strip leading zeros last.
edge_cases: Leftover k after the pass means the digits were already increasing - remove from the END.
Leading zeros must be stripped, and an empty result becomes '0'.
k equal to the length returns '0'.

complexity.why: each digit is pushed and popped once. The combinatorial choice of which k digits to remove is exponential, which is what the greedy replaces.

followups.q: Prove the greedy is correct.
followups.a: If d[i] > d[i+1], removing d[i] reduces the digit at the most significant differing position, which dominates every lower place. So it is never worse to remove it.

followups.q: Maximise the number instead.
followups.a: Flip the stack direction to decreasing. Same algorithm.

followups.q: Remove duplicate letters keeping lexicographic minimality.
followups.a: LC 316 - same monotonic stack, plus a last-occurrence table so you never pop a letter that will not reappear.

learnings.insight: Do not enumerate subarrays. Count each element's CONTRIBUTION: a[i] is the minimum of exactly left * right subarrays, where left is the distance to the previous smaller element and right the distance to the next smaller. That reframing is the whole problem.
learnings.trick: Two monotonic stack passes give previous-smaller and next-smaller boundaries. Answer is the sum of a[i] * left * right, taken modulo 1e9+7.
edge_cases: Duplicates must use strict comparison on one side and non-strict on the other, or identical subarrays are counted twice.
Products overflow int - accumulate in long long and reduce modulo at each step.
Elements with no smaller neighbour extend to the array boundary.

complexity.why: two linear stack passes. Enumerating all subarrays is O(n^2) and exceeds the limits.

followups.q: Explain the duplicate handling.
followups.a: If both sides used strict comparison, a subarray whose minimum appears twice would be counted for each occurrence. Making one side non-strict assigns it to exactly one.

followups.q: Sum of subarray ranges.
followups.a: LC 2104 - run the same computation for maxima and subtract the minima total. Two applications of one idea.

learnings.insight: Range equals maximum minus minimum, and summation is linear, so the total equals the sum of all subarray maxima minus the sum of all subarray minima. Two runs of the previous problem, one with the comparison flipped.
learnings.trick: Write one contribution-counting routine parameterised by the comparator, then call it twice and subtract.
edge_cases: The O(n^2) brute force actually passes here given small constraints - but the O(n) solution is the point of the exercise.
Duplicate handling must be consistent between the two runs.
Sums overflow int - use long long throughout.

complexity.why: four monotonic stack passes in total, all linear. The brute force is O(n^2).

followups.q: Why does linearity let you split the sum?
followups.a: Sum over subarrays of (max - min) equals sum of maxes minus sum of mins, because summation distributes over subtraction. Many aggregate problems decompose this way.

followups.q: Sum of subarray medians.
followups.a: Does not decompose - medians are not linear. This is exactly the boundary where the trick stops working.

learnings.insight: For each bar, the widest rectangle of that height extends left to the previous shorter bar and right to the next shorter one. A single increasing stack produces both boundaries in one pass - when a bar is popped, the new top is its left boundary and the current index is its right.
learnings.trick: Append a sentinel height of 0 to force the stack to drain. Width is i - stackTopAfterPop - 1, which correctly handles the case where the stack empties.
edge_cases: Without the sentinel you need a separate drain loop after the main pass.
When the stack empties after a pop, the left boundary is -1, so width is simply i.
Equal heights can use either comparison; the maximum is unaffected.

complexity.why: each bar is pushed and popped once. The O(n^2) approach expanding from each bar is what this replaces.

followups.q: Maximal rectangle in a binary matrix.
followups.a: LC 85 - run this once per row, treating consecutive ones above each row as histogram heights. O(m*n) total.

followups.q: Why does the popped element's width extend past the current top?
followups.a: Everything between them was taller and already popped, so the popped bar's height is valid across that whole span.

followups.q: Divide and conquer alternative.
followups.a: Recurse on the minimum bar, O(n log n) average but O(n^2) worst on sorted input. The stack is strictly better.

learnings.insight: A heap gives O(n log k) but cannot cheaply remove elements leaving the window. A monotonic deque can, because any element smaller than a later arrival is permanently irrelevant and can be discarded immediately.
learnings.trick: Deque of indices with decreasing values. Evict from the front when the index falls out of the window; evict from the back while the new value dominates. The front is always the window maximum.
edge_cases: Store indices so the out-of-window check is possible.
Front eviction must come before back eviction to keep the window valid.
Start recording answers only once i >= k-1.

complexity.why: each index is pushed and popped exactly once, so the two inner whiles contribute O(n) in total. The heap solution is O(n log k) with lazy deletion.

followups.q: Why is a smaller earlier element permanently irrelevant?
followups.a: It leaves the window no later than the larger newer one, and it is smaller, so it can never be the maximum while the newer element is present.

followups.q: Sliding window MEDIAN.
followups.a: The deque trick does not apply - medians need order statistics. Use two heaps with lazy deletion, or a multiset with an iterator to the middle. LC 480.

followups.q: Sliding window minimum.
followups.a: Flip the comparison. The deque becomes increasing.

problems.title: Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String

learnings.insight: Removing a pair can create a new adjacent pair, so repeated scanning is O(n^2). A stack handles the cascade naturally: the element you just pushed is exactly the one the next character must be compared against.
learnings.trick: Use the output string itself as the stack. If the last character equals the incoming one, pop it; otherwise push. One pass, no separate container.
edge_cases: The cascade is the point - 'abbaca' becomes 'ca' only because removing 'bb' exposes 'aa'.
An empty result is valid.
Building into the result string directly avoids a final reversal.

complexity.why: each character is pushed and popped at most once. The repeated-scan approach is O(n^2).

followups.q: Remove groups of exactly k adjacent duplicates.
followups.a: LC 1209 - stack of (character, count) pairs, popping when the count reaches k. Same idea with a counter attached.

followups.q: Why can't you just scan repeatedly?
followups.a: Each pass may remove only one pair while exposing another, so you can need O(n) passes of O(n) work.

learnings.insight: Building both strings with stacks is the obvious O(n) solution. The interesting version is O(1) space, which requires scanning from the RIGHT - because a backspace affects what came before it, which is only knowable in advance when moving backwards.
learnings.trick: Two pointers from the ends. At each, skip backwards counting '#' and consuming that many real characters, then compare the surviving characters.
edge_cases: More backspaces than characters is valid and consumes nothing further.
Both pointers may run off the start simultaneously, which means equality.
One string exhausting before the other means inequality.

complexity.why: each character is examined once per pointer. The stack solution is the same time but O(n) space, which the follow-up rules out.

followups.q: Why must the O(1) solution scan from the right?
followups.a: A backspace deletes the character before it, so moving left to right you cannot know whether a character survives until you have read further. From the right, the backspaces are already known.

followups.q: Return the resulting string instead of comparing.
followups.a: Then O(n) space is unavoidable, because the output itself is that large.

learnings.insight: A pure stack simulation with four operation types. There is no algorithmic content - it exists to check that you can translate a specification into code without mis-ordering the operand handling.
learnings.trick: Push integers. 'D' pushes twice the top, 'C' pops, '+' pushes the sum of the top two - which requires peeking two deep without permanently removing either.
edge_cases: '+' must not consume its operands - pop, read, push back, or index the underlying vector.
Using a vector rather than std::stack makes two-deep access trivial.
The input is guaranteed valid, so no underflow checks are needed.

complexity.why: one pass with constant work per operation.

followups.q: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation.
followups.a: LC 150 - the same stack shape with genuine arithmetic operators. Watch the operand order for subtraction and division: the second popped value is the left operand.

learnings.insight: Trust is a directed graph, and the judge is the unique node with in-degree n-1 and out-degree 0. Framing it that way replaces any search with two counting arrays.
learnings.trick: A single balance array: trusting someone decrements your score, being trusted increments theirs. The judge is the unique node with balance exactly n-1.
edge_cases: n = 1 with no trust relationships makes person 1 the judge.
No valid judge returns -1.
The judge must trust nobody, which the decrement enforces automatically.

complexity.why: one pass over the edges and one over the nodes. No graph traversal is needed at all.

followups.q: Why does a single balance array suffice?
followups.a: Only the judge can reach n-1, since anyone who trusts someone loses a point and can reach at most n-2. So the combined score uniquely identifies them.

followups.q: Find the centre of a star graph.
followups.a: LC 1791 - the centre appears in both of the first two edges, so it is O(1) with no counting at all.

learnings.insight: A fixed-size window needs no shrink loop at all - each step adds the entering element and removes the leaving one. This is the simplest possible window and the right place to internalise that structure.
learnings.trick: Build the first window explicitly, then slide with sum += a[r] - a[r-k]. Compare sums rather than averages to avoid floating-point comparison entirely.
edge_cases: Divide only once at the end - comparing averages in a loop invites precision errors.
k equal to n means a single window.
Sums of 1e5 values at 1e4 fit in int, but long long costs nothing.

complexity.why: one pass with two operations per step. Recomputing each window's sum is O(n*k).

followups.q: Why compare sums rather than averages?
followups.a: All windows share the divisor k, so the ordering is identical and integer comparison is exact. Dividing early introduces rounding for no benefit.

followups.q: Maximum average of any subarray of length AT LEAST k.
followups.a: LC 644 - binary search on the answer, checking feasibility with a prefix-sum sweep. Much harder, and a good example of how 'at least' changes everything.

learnings.insight: A fixed window on a circular array. The modulo handles the wrap, and a negative k simply means the window sits behind each index rather than ahead of it.
learnings.trick: Handle k = 0 by returning zeros. Otherwise build one window and slide it, indexing with (i % n + n) % n so negative offsets behave.
edge_cases: k = 0 returns an all-zero array, not the input.
Negative k reads backwards - the same loop with a shifted start.
The double modulo is needed because C++ % of a negative value is negative.

complexity.why: a constant-size window slid n times. The naive nested version is O(n*k).

followups.q: Why the double modulo?
followups.a: In C++, -1 % 5 is -1, not 4. Adding n before the second modulo normalises it into range - the same fix used in hash functions with negative keys.

learnings.insight: Squaring destroys the sort order because negatives become large. But the LARGEST square is always at one end or the other, so filling the output from the back with two converging pointers restores order in one pass.
learnings.trick: Pointers at both ends, write position at the end of the output. Compare absolute values and write the larger square, moving that pointer inward.
edge_cases: All negatives means the output is the reversed squares.
Compare absolute values, or compare squares directly - either works, squares avoid abs().
Fill the output backwards; filling forwards requires knowing the smallest first, which is in the middle.

complexity.why: each pointer moves inward once. Squaring then sorting is O(n log n) and throws away the input's sortedness.

followups.q: Why fill backwards?
followups.a: The maximum square is at a known position - one of the two ends - while the minimum is somewhere in the middle and would have to be searched for.

followups.q: Do it in O(1) extra space.
followups.a: Not possible in general, since the output must be a new array. If in-place modification were allowed you could partition at zero and merge in place.

learnings.insight: Greedily matching the earliest possible occurrence of each character is optimal - taking a later match can never help, since it only shrinks what remains. That exchange argument is why a single pass suffices.
learnings.trick: One pointer per string. Advance the s-pointer only on a match, always advance the t-pointer. Success is the s-pointer reaching the end.
edge_cases: Empty s is a subsequence of anything.
s longer than t can be rejected immediately.
The follow-up about many queries is the real question here.

complexity.why: each pointer advances monotonically. The DP formulation is O(n*m) and unnecessary for a single query.

followups.q: Billions of queries against the same t.
followups.a: Precompute, for each position in t and each letter, the next occurrence of that letter. Each query then costs O(|s| log |t|) or O(|s|) depending on the index structure.

followups.q: Prove the greedy match is optimal.
followups.a: If a solution matches s[i] at position p, any earlier valid position p' < p leaves a superset of t available for the rest of s. So taking the earliest is never worse.

learnings.insight: On the first mismatch there are exactly two possibilities - delete the left character or the right - and each can be checked in linear time. Because only one deletion is allowed, the branching happens at most once, so the whole thing stays O(n).
learnings.trick: Walk inward until a mismatch. Then test whether either s[l+1..r] or s[l..r-1] is a plain palindrome. No recursion or backtracking needed.
edge_cases: Already a palindrome returns true without any deletion.
The branch happens at most once - that is what bounds the complexity.
Single character and empty strings are palindromes.

complexity.why: one inward scan plus at most two linear verification scans. Allowing k deletions would make the branching exponential and force a DP.

followups.q: At most k deletions.
followups.a: The branching becomes exponential, so switch to DP: the answer is yes when the longest palindromic subsequence has length at least n - k.

followups.q: Why does the branch occur only once?
followups.a: The deletion budget is one. After spending it, the remainder must match exactly, so no further branching is possible.

learnings.insight: A plain seen-set answers 'is there a duplicate anywhere'. Bounding the distance turns it into a windowed set - evict elements as they fall out of range, so membership implicitly means 'within k'.
learnings.trick: Maintain an unordered_set of the last k elements. Before inserting index i, erase index i-k-1 if it exists. Any successful membership test is then automatically within range.
edge_cases: k = 0 can never satisfy the distance condition.
Eviction must happen before the membership test, or a stale element gives a false positive.
k larger than n degrades to plain Contains Duplicate.

complexity.why: one pass with O(1) average set operations, and the set never exceeds k elements. The last-index map alternative is O(n) space but avoids eviction logic.

followups.q: Bound the VALUE difference too.
followups.a: LC 220 - a set alone is insufficient; you need an ordered structure to find the nearest value, or bucketing by value range for O(n).

followups.q: The last-index map alternative.
followups.a: Store value to most recent index and compare i - lastIndex <= k. No eviction needed, but O(n) space rather than O(k).

learnings.insight: A fixed window of 10 characters plus a hash set of what has been seen. The interesting part is the follow-up: each nucleotide needs only 2 bits, so a 10-length window fits in 20 bits and can be rolled in O(1) as an integer.
learnings.trick: Map A, C, G, T to 0-3. Roll a 20-bit integer with `code = ((code << 2) | v) & 0xFFFFF`. Count occurrences and report anything seen exactly twice, to avoid duplicate output.
edge_cases: Report on the SECOND occurrence only, or a sequence appearing three times is emitted twice.
Strings shorter than 10 return empty.
The mask 0xFFFFF keeps exactly 20 bits.

complexity.why: one pass with constant-time rolling and hashing. Storing substrings directly is O(10n) space and slower to hash.

followups.q: Why 2 bits per character?
followups.a: There are exactly four nucleotides, so two bits encode each. Ten characters therefore fit in 20 bits, well inside an int.

followups.q: Generalise to length L over an arbitrary alphabet.
followups.a: Polynomial rolling hash with a large prime modulus, verifying hits to guard against collisions.

learnings.insight: Structurally identical to 3Sum, but because you can never exit early on an exact match, the sweep always runs to completion. Tracking the best difference replaces the equality test.
learnings.trick: Sort, fix an anchor, converge two pointers. Update the best whenever the absolute difference improves, and move the pointer in the direction that reduces the gap.
edge_cases: An exact match can be returned immediately as an optimisation.
Sums overflow int with large values - accumulate in long long.
Duplicate skipping is optional here since only one answer is returned.

complexity.why: sort plus a nested sweep, each anchor's inner pass being linear.

followups.q: Why can't you skip duplicates aggressively?
followups.a: You can, and it is a safe optimisation - but unlike 3Sum it is not required for correctness, since only the closest value is reported.

followups.q: k-Sum closest.
followups.a: The same recursive reduction as kSum, with the closest-tracking pushed into the two-pointer base case.

learnings.insight: Two nested anchors reduce this to Two Sum on the remainder. The real content is overflow - four values near 1e9 sum past int - and deduplication at three separate levels rather than two.
learnings.trick: Sort, two nested loops with duplicate skips at both levels, then converging pointers. Accumulate the sum in long long from the first addition.
edge_cases: Sums overflow int; cast before adding, not after.
Duplicate skips are needed at both anchor levels AND at both pointers.
Pruning on the smallest and largest possible remaining sums cuts a lot of work.

complexity.why: two nested anchors with a linear inner sweep. The general kSum reduction gives O(n^(k-1)).

followups.q: Write a general kSum.
followups.a: Recurse: for k > 2, loop an anchor and recurse on k-1; at k = 2 use two pointers. Clean, and it makes the O(n^(k-1)) bound obvious.

followups.q: 4Sum II, with four separate arrays.
followups.a: LC 454 - hash the pairwise sums of the first two arrays, then look up complements from the other two. O(n^2) rather than O(n^3), because the arrays are independent.

learnings.insight: 'Two baskets' is 'at most two distinct values in the window' wearing a story. Stripping the narrative to the constraint is the actual skill - and once stripped, it is a textbook variable window with a frequency map.
learnings.trick: Expand right, incrementing the count for the new fruit. While the map holds more than two keys, advance left and ERASE any key whose count reaches zero - otherwise map.size() is wrong.
edge_cases: Erasing zero-count keys is mandatory; without it the size check never triggers correctly.
Fewer than three distinct fruits overall means the answer is the whole array.
The answer is a count of fruits, which is the window length.

complexity.space: O(1) since at most three keys are ever held
complexity.why: each index enters and leaves once. The map holds at most k+1 entries, so its operations are effectively constant.

followups.q: Generalise to k baskets.
followups.a: Replace 2 with k. That is LC 340, which is premium - this problem is the free instance of it.

followups.q: Why must zero-count keys be erased?
followups.a: unordered_map::size() counts keys, not non-zero values. A key left at zero keeps inflating the distinct count and the window never shrinks correctly.

learnings.insight: Counting subarrays with sum EXACTLY goal is awkward with a window, because the shrink condition is ambiguous when zeros are present. atMost(goal) - atMost(goal-1) sidesteps it entirely and is the reusable idea here.
learnings.trick: Write one helper counting subarrays with sum at most k by accumulating (r - l + 1) at each right endpoint, then subtract the two calls.
edge_cases: goal = 0 requires atMost(-1) to return 0 - guard the helper.
Zeros are what make the direct window ambiguous, since they extend a window without changing its sum.
The prefix-count map alternative is equally valid and worth knowing.

complexity.why: two linear passes. The prefix-sum map solution is also O(n) but uses O(n) space.

followups.q: Why is the direct window ambiguous?
followups.a: With a run of zeros, many left positions give the same sum, so 'shrink while too large' does not identify a unique window and counting becomes error-prone.

followups.q: Solve it with prefix sums.
followups.a: It is exactly Subarray Sum Equals K on a 0/1 array. Recognising that two problems are the same is worth more than either solution.

learnings.insight: The definitive example of the atMost decomposition. A window for exactly k distinct values has no valid shrink rule, but atMost(k) is routine - and exactly(k) is the difference of two such counts.
learnings.trick: atMost(k) counts subarrays with at most k distinct values by accumulating (r - l + 1). Return atMost(k) - atMost(k-1).
edge_cases: Erase zero-count keys or the distinct count is wrong.
k = 1 still needs atMost(0), which must return 0.
Accumulating (r - l + 1) counts every valid subarray ending at r, not just the longest.

complexity.why: two linear passes, each with a map bounded by k+1 entries.

followups.q: Prove the subtraction is correct.
followups.a: Every subarray with at most k distinct values is counted once in the first term. Those with at most k-1 appear in both terms and cancel. What survives has exactly k.

followups.q: Why does accumulating (r - l + 1) count correctly?
followups.a: For a valid window [l, r], every subarray ending at r and starting at or after l is also valid, because removing elements from the left cannot increase the distinct count.

problems.title: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters

tuf.striver_title: Number of Substrings Containing All Three Characters

learnings.insight: Rather than maintaining a window, track the last index at which each of a, b and c appeared. Every substring ending at i and starting at or before the minimum of those three contains all of them.
learnings.trick: Keep last[3]. At each i, add `min(last[0], last[1], last[2]) + 1` to the answer, which counts all valid starting positions at once.
edge_cases: Initialise last[] to -1 so the +1 makes the contribution zero before all three appear.
The answer can exceed int for long strings - use long long.
Only three characters appear, by constraint.

complexity.why: one pass with three scalars. The standard sliding window also works in O(n); this variant is shorter and avoids the map entirely.

followups.q: Solve it with a conventional window instead.
followups.a: Shrink from the left while all three remain present, and add (l + 1) at each step. Equivalent, and it generalises to larger alphabets more naturally.

followups.q: Generalise to an arbitrary required set.
followups.a: The last-occurrence trick needs the minimum over the whole required set, which is O(k) per step unless you maintain it - at which point the window is cleaner.

problems.title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards

tuf.striver_title: Maximum Points You Can Obtain from Cards

learnings.insight: Choosing k cards from the two ends is the same as LEAVING a contiguous window of n-k cards in the middle. Maximising what you take equals minimising what you leave, and the complement is a fixed-size window.
learnings.trick: Compute the total, then find the minimum sum of any window of size n-k. The answer is total minus that minimum.
edge_cases: k = n means taking everything; the complement window has size zero.
The direct approach - sliding a prefix/suffix split - also works and is equally valid.
Sums fit in int here but long long costs nothing.

complexity.why: one pass for the total and one for the minimum window. Enumerating all 2^k choices of ends is exponential; even the prefix/suffix version is O(k).

followups.q: Solve it without the complement.
followups.a: Take k from the front, then repeatedly swap one front card for one back card, tracking the best. O(k) and arguably more direct.

followups.q: Why is the complement a contiguous window?
followups.a: Taking cards only from the ends means what remains is always an unbroken middle segment - which is exactly a window.

problems.title: Frequency of the Most Frequent Element

tuf.striver_title: Highest Occurring Element in an Array

learnings.insight: You would always raise smaller elements up to a larger one, never the reverse - so sorting first makes the target the window's right end. The cost of levelling a window is then (windowLength * target) minus the window's sum, which is a prefix-sum computation.
learnings.trick: Sort, then slide a window. Shrink while `(long long)a[r] * (r - l + 1) - windowSum > k`. The multiplication overflows int, so cast.
edge_cases: a[r] * windowLength overflows int at 1e5 elements of 1e5 - cast to long long.
k operations are total, not per element.
The answer is the window length, not the value.

complexity.why: the sort dominates; the window pass is linear. Without sorting there is no way to identify the target cheaply.

followups.q: Why sort first?
followups.a: Raising a larger element to match a smaller one is never useful, so the target of any optimal window is its maximum. Sorting puts that at the right edge, making the cost formula closed-form.

followups.q: Binary search alternative.
followups.a: The answer is monotone - if a frequency f is achievable, so is f-1 - so you can binary search the answer and check feasibility with a fixed window. Same bound, different route.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array

learnings.insight: Sorting is O(n log n) and answers far more than was asked. The two better options are a size-k MIN-heap at O(n log k), and quickselect at O(n) average - and knowing when each is correct is the actual question.
learnings.trick: For the k LARGEST, keep a MIN-heap of size k. The inversion is deliberate: the weakest of your current winners sits on top, ready to be evicted in O(log k).
edge_cases: k is 1-indexed; k = 1 is the maximum.
Duplicates count toward k - the 2nd largest of [3,3,1] is 3.
Pop only when the size EXCEEDS k, not when it equals k.

complexity.time: O(n log k) with the heap, O(n) average with quickselect
complexity.why: each of n elements costs O(log k) to insert and possibly evict. Quickselect recurses into only one partition, giving T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n).

followups.q: Why a min-heap for the k largest?
followups.a: You repeatedly need to discard the WORST of your current best k. A min-heap keeps that at the root; a max-heap would make finding it O(k).

followups.q: Data does not fit in memory.
followups.a: Quickselect needs random access to the whole array, so it is unavailable. The size-k heap streams and uses only O(k) space - that constraint is what decides between them.

followups.q: Worst-case O(n).
followups.a: Median-of-medians pivot selection makes quickselect worst-case linear, at the cost of a large constant that makes it slower in practice.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream

tuf.striver_title: Kth largest element in a stream of running integers

learnings.insight: The streaming version of the previous problem, and it makes the size-k heap's advantage concrete: quickselect cannot apply because there is no complete array to partition.
learnings.trick: Keep a min-heap capped at k. Every add pushes and pops down to size k, then returns the root. Seed it with the initial array the same way.
edge_cases: The initial array may be shorter than k - the heap simply fills up over time.
Pop after pushing, not before, or you evict the wrong element.
Duplicates are retained; they count toward k.

complexity.why: each insertion is one push and at most one pop on a heap of size k.

followups.q: Why can't quickselect be used here?
followups.a: It requires the full array in memory to partition, and it destroys the ordering. A stream offers neither.

followups.q: Kth SMALLEST in a stream.
followups.a: Symmetric - a max-heap of size k.

learnings.insight: A direct simulation where the only requirement is repeatedly extracting the two largest elements - which is precisely what a max-heap provides in O(log n).
learnings.trick: Push everything into a max-heap. While more than one remains, pop two and push back the difference if it is non-zero.
edge_cases: Equal stones destroy each other completely - push nothing back.
An empty heap at the end means 0.
A single stone is returned unchanged.

complexity.why: n insertions and at most n extractions, each O(log n). Sorting after every collision would be O(n^2 log n).

followups.q: Last Stone Weight II - minimise the final stone.
followups.a: Completely different. Partition the stones into two groups with sums as close as possible, which is subset-sum DP. Same story, different problem.

followups.q: Why a heap rather than sorting once?
followups.a: The pushed-back difference must be reinserted in order, and repeated sorting is far more expensive than a heap's O(log n) insert.

problems.title: The K Weakest Rows in a Matrix

learnings.insight: Each row is sorted, so its soldier count is a binary search rather than a scan. Combine that with a size-k heap on (strength, index) pairs and neither dimension is handled naively.
learnings.trick: Binary search each row for the first zero to get its count in O(log n), then keep a max-heap of size k on (count, index) so ties break by index.
edge_cases: Ties must break by row index, which a pair comparison gives for free.
A row may be all ones or all zeros - the binary search must handle both bounds.
k is at most the number of rows.

complexity.time: O(m log n + m log k)
complexity.why: one binary search per row plus heap operations bounded by k. Counting each row linearly would be O(m*n).

followups.q: Why does a pair comparison break ties correctly?
followups.a: std::pair compares lexicographically, so equal counts fall back to the index - exactly the required ordering.

followups.q: Rows are not sorted.
followups.a: Binary search is unavailable; counting becomes O(n) per row for O(m*n) total.

learnings.insight: Count first, then select. The heap gives O(n log k), but frequencies are bounded by n, which means bucket sort gives O(n) - the same instinct as counting sort, and the follow-up the question is really after.
learnings.trick: Bucket by frequency: an array of n+1 vectors indexed by count, filled from the frequency map, then read from the highest index down until k elements are collected.
edge_cases: Bucket array needs n+1 slots, since a frequency can equal n.
Ties may be returned in any order here.
Stop as soon as k elements are collected, not after draining every bucket.

complexity.time: O(n) with bucketing, O(n log k) with a heap
complexity.why: counting is linear and bucketing is linear because the frequency range is bounded. The heap version pays a log factor to avoid the extra array.

followups.q: Make it O(n).
followups.a: Bucket sort by frequency. The bound on frequencies is the constraint that makes it possible - the same reasoning as counting sort.

followups.q: Top K Frequent WORDS with lexicographic tie-breaking.
followups.a: LC 692 - a heap with a custom comparator, since bucketing alone cannot order ties.

followups.q: Quickselect alternative.
followups.a: Partition the (value, count) pairs on count. O(n) average, O(1) extra space beyond the map.

learnings.insight: The nth ugly number cannot be found by testing candidates - they thin out too fast. Instead GENERATE them: every ugly number is a previous one multiplied by 2, 3 or 5, so the sequence is a three-way merge of itself.
learnings.trick: Three pointers into the sequence being built, each tracking the next multiple of 2, 3 and 5. Take the minimum and advance EVERY pointer that produced it, which is how duplicates are avoided.
edge_cases: Advancing only one pointer on a tie produces duplicates - 6 is both 2*3 and 3*2.
The first ugly number is 1.
Values fit in int for n = 1690, which is the constraint limit.

complexity.why: one constant-time step per generated number. The heap version is O(n log n) and needs a set to deduplicate - the pointer version avoids both.

followups.q: Why advance every matching pointer?
followups.a: Because the same value can be produced by several factors. Advancing only one leaves the others pointing at a value already emitted.

followups.q: Arbitrary set of primes.
followups.a: LC 313 - k pointers instead of three, or a min-heap when k is large enough that scanning the pointers dominates.

learnings.insight: The generalisation of Ugly Number II from three factors to k. The structure is unchanged; only the number of pointers grows, and at some k a heap becomes cheaper than scanning them all.
learnings.trick: Keep one pointer per prime. Each step scans the k candidates for the minimum, emits it, and advances every pointer that produced it.
edge_cases: Duplicate handling is identical - advance all matching pointers.
Intermediate products can overflow int; use long long for the candidates.
k can reach 100, at which point the O(n*k) scan is still fine but a heap is competitive.

complexity.why: each of n numbers requires scanning k pointers. A min-heap makes it O(n log k), which wins for large k.

followups.q: When does the heap become worthwhile?
followups.a: When log k is smaller than k - in practice around k = 20 or more. Below that the linear scan has a better constant.

followups.q: Why not generate and sort?
followups.a: The products explode combinatorially; you cannot bound how many to generate without already knowing the nth value.

learnings.insight: The heap simulation works, but there is a closed form: the most frequent task builds a skeleton of (maxFreq - 1) blocks each of length (n + 1), and every other task fills the idle slots. Deriving that formula is a far stronger answer than simulating.
learnings.trick: answer = max(taskCount, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + countOfTasksWithMaxFreq). The max() handles the case where there are so many distinct tasks that no idling is ever needed.
edge_cases: When enough distinct tasks exist, the answer is simply the task count - hence the max().
Several tasks may share the maximum frequency; all of them occupy the final block.
n = 0 means no cooldown, so the answer is the task count.

complexity.why: one counting pass and a formula. The heap simulation is O(total time * log 26), which is correct but slower and harder to reason about.

followups.q: Derive the formula.
followups.a: Lay out the most frequent task maxFreq times, separated by n slots: that is (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) time, plus one slot for each task tied at maxFreq in the final block. Other tasks fill idle slots without extending the total.

followups.q: Return the actual schedule, not just its length.
followups.a: Now you need the heap simulation - the formula gives the length but not the ordering.

followups.q: Why the max() with task count?
followups.a: With many distinct tasks the idle slots are all filled and the schedule is fully packed, so the total is just the number of tasks.

learnings.insight: The smallest remaining card MUST begin a group - nothing smaller exists to precede it. That forced choice makes the greedy exact, and it removes any need to search over groupings.
learnings.trick: Count into an ordered map. Repeatedly take the smallest key, and consume one of each of the next groupSize consecutive values, failing if any is missing.
edge_cases: n % groupSize != 0 means failure - check before doing any work.
Erase keys when their count reaches zero, or the smallest key is stale.
Counts can exceed one, so consume exactly one per group rather than clearing.

complexity.why: each card is consumed once, with O(log n) map operations. The greedy is exact because the smallest card's group is forced.

followups.q: Prove the greedy.
followups.a: The smallest remaining card has no possible predecessor, so it must be the first element of its group. Its group is then fully determined, leaving a strictly smaller instance.

followups.q: Split Array into Consecutive Subsequences.
followups.a: LC 659 - similar but groups may be longer than the minimum, so a greedy with two counters (available and ending-here) is needed instead.

learnings.insight: A design problem whose core is a k-way merge: each user's feed is the merge of their own and their followees' tweet lists, and you only need the ten newest. Storing tweets newest-first makes each list a sorted sequence.
learnings.trick: Per-user vector of (timestamp, tweetId) and a set of followees. getNewsFeed pushes the head of each relevant list into a heap and pops ten times, refilling from the same list each time.
edge_cases: A user follows themselves implicitly for feed purposes - handle it or add them to the set.
Unfollowing yourself must not be permitted.
Only the last ten tweets per user are ever needed, which bounds the work.

complexity.time: O(f log f + 10 log f) per feed
complexity.why: the heap holds one entry per followed user, so operations are logarithmic in the follow count rather than the tweet count.

followups.q: Millions of followees.
followups.a: Fan-out-on-write instead: push each tweet into followers' precomputed feeds at post time. Trades write cost for read cost, which is what real systems do.

followups.q: Why is a global timestamp needed?
followups.a: Tweets must be merged in chronological order across users, and per-user indices are not comparable.

learnings.insight: This is coordinate compression, a preprocessing step used constantly in segment-tree and DP problems. Map each distinct value to its position in the sorted order of distinct values.
learnings.trick: Copy, sort, unique-erase to get distinct values, then rank each original element with lower_bound. Ranks are 1-indexed here.
edge_cases: Duplicates must receive the SAME rank, which is why the dedup step matters.
Empty input returns empty.
Ranks start at 1, not 0.

complexity.why: the sort dominates, with an O(log n) lookup per element. A map from value to rank is an equivalent formulation.

followups.q: Where is coordinate compression actually needed?
followups.a: Whenever values are huge but few - segment trees or Fenwick trees indexed by value, sweep lines over coordinates, and DP keyed on values. It converts a 1e9 range into an n-sized one.

followups.q: Do it without sorting.
followups.a: Not in better than O(n log n) in general, since producing ranks is equivalent to sorting.

learnings.insight: Split the data into a lower half and an upper half, each kept as a heap facing inward. The median then sits at the tops. The difficulty is not the idea but keeping the invariant that every element in the lower half is at most every element in the upper.
learnings.trick: Always push to the max-heap, immediately move its top to the min-heap, then rebalance sizes if the min-heap has grown larger. Three unconditional operations, no case analysis.
edge_cases: Naively pushing to whichever heap 'looks right' breaks the ordering invariant.
Odd totals leave the extra element in the max-heap by convention.
Use double division for the even case, or integer division truncates.

complexity.time: O(log n) per insertion, O(1) per query
complexity.why: each insertion performs a constant number of heap operations. A sorted container with insertion is O(n) per add.

followups.q: Numbers are all in 0-100.
followups.a: A 101-slot count array plus a running total gives O(1) insertion and O(100) median - counting sort again.

followups.q: 99% of values are in a narrow range.
followups.a: Bucket the common range and keep overflow lists for outliers.

followups.q: Sliding window median.
followups.a: LC 480 - two heaps plus lazy deletion via a to-remove map, or a multiset with an iterator kept at the middle. Removal is what makes it substantially harder.

learnings.insight: Satisfy the least greedy child with the smallest adequate cookie. Spending a large cookie on a small appetite wastes capacity that a greedier child could have used - that exchange argument is why the greedy is exact.
learnings.trick: Sort both arrays, then walk two pointers. Advance the cookie pointer always; advance the child pointer only on a successful assignment.
edge_cases: More children than cookies, or vice versa - the loop guard handles both.
A cookie too small for the current child is too small for every later one, so it is discarded permanently.
Empty input on either side gives 0.

complexity.time: O(n log n + m log m)
complexity.why: the two sorts dominate; the sweep is linear. Without sorting there is no basis for the greedy choice.

followups.q: Prove the exchange argument.
followups.a: If an optimal solution gives child c a cookie larger than needed while a smaller adequate one is unused, swapping them keeps the solution valid and frees the larger cookie. Repeating this reaches the greedy solution without loss.

followups.q: Maximise total satisfaction rather than the count.
followups.a: Greedy fails; it becomes an assignment problem solvable by min-cost matching.

learnings.insight: When giving change for a twenty, prefer a ten plus a five over three fives. Fives are more flexible - they can pay change for tens as well - so spending the inflexible note first preserves options.
learnings.trick: Count fives and tens only; twenties are never given as change. For a twenty, try 10+5 first and fall back to 5+5+5.
edge_cases: The order of the two options for a twenty is the whole problem.
The first customer paying anything other than five fails immediately.
Twenties never re-enter circulation.

complexity.why: one pass with two counters.

followups.q: Why prefer 10+5?
followups.a: A five can serve as change for both a ten and a twenty, while a ten only helps with a twenty. Spending the less versatile note first is the greedy invariant.

followups.q: Arbitrary denominations.
followups.a: Greedy fails in general - it becomes the coin change problem, which needs DP.

learnings.insight: To maximise the sum of pair minimums, pair each element with its nearest neighbour in sorted order. Pairing distant elements wastes the larger one, since only the smaller of each pair counts.
learnings.trick: Sort, then sum every element at an even index. No explicit pairing is needed.
edge_cases: The array length is guaranteed even.
Negative numbers work unchanged.
Values are bounded at 1e4, so counting sort gives O(n) if you want it.

complexity.why: the sort dominates; the sum is linear. With bounded values, counting sort makes it O(n + k).

followups.q: Prove pairing adjacent elements is optimal.
followups.a: If a < b < c < d are paired as (a,c) and (b,d), the sum is a + b. Repairing as (a,b) and (c,d) gives a + c, which is larger. So any non-adjacent pairing can be improved.

followups.q: Make it O(n).
followups.a: Counting sort, since values lie in [-1e4, 1e4].

learnings.insight: This is fractional knapsack with unit-sized items: take the highest-value boxes first. It is greedy and exact precisely because boxes are interchangeable within a type and can be taken partially in count.
learnings.trick: Sort descending by units per box, then take boxes until the truck is full.
edge_cases: The last type is usually taken partially - take min(remaining, available).
Truck size may exceed the total boxes.
Sorting ascending and iterating backwards is equivalent.

complexity.why: the sort dominates. This is the greedy that works BECAUSE the items are divisible by count - 0/1 knapsack with indivisible items would need DP.

followups.q: Why is 0/1 knapsack not greedy?
followups.a: Indivisible items break the exchange argument - taking the highest-density item may exclude a combination that fills the capacity better. Divisibility restores it.

followups.q: Boxes have both weight and volume limits.
followups.a: Two constraints make it multidimensional knapsack, which is NP-hard.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Moves to Seat Everyone

learnings.insight: Matching the ith smallest student to the ith smallest seat minimises the total distance. Any crossing assignment can be uncrossed without increasing the cost, which is a standard rearrangement argument.
learnings.trick: Sort both arrays and sum the absolute differences at matching indices.
edge_cases: The arrays are guaranteed equal length.
Positions may coincide, contributing zero.
Values are bounded at 100, so counting sort applies.

complexity.why: two sorts and a linear sum.

followups.q: Prove sorted matching is optimal.
