followups.a: If a < b are matched to y > x, then |a-y| + |b-x| >= |a-x| + |b-y|. So uncrossing never increases the total, and the fully sorted matching is reached by repeated uncrossing.

followups.q: Minimise the MAXIMUM move instead.
followups.a: Still sorted matching, but take the maximum rather than the sum - the same pairing is optimal for both objectives.

learnings.insight: A palindrome uses characters in pairs, with at most one odd character allowed in the centre. So the answer is the sum of the even parts of every count, plus one if any count was odd.
learnings.trick: Sum (count / 2) * 2 across all characters, then add 1 if any count was odd. No construction is needed.
edge_cases: Only ONE odd-count character may sit in the centre, regardless of how many exist.
Case-sensitive - 'A' and 'a' are different characters.
A string of all distinct characters gives 1.

complexity.why: one counting pass over a fixed alphabet.

followups.q: Why can only one odd character be used?
followups.a: Every character except the exact centre must have a mirror. A second unmatched character has nowhere to sit.

followups.q: Construct the palindrome rather than measure it.
followups.a: Build half from the paired characters, place the odd one in the middle, then mirror.

problems.title: Maximize Sum Of Array After K Negations

learnings.insight: Flip the most negative values first, since each flip gains twice their magnitude. Once no negatives remain, any leftover flips should be spent repeatedly on the smallest absolute value - and only their parity matters.
learnings.trick: Sort ascending, flip negatives while k remains. Then if k is still positive and odd, subtract twice the minimum absolute value from the total.
edge_cases: Leftover k with even parity costs nothing - flipping twice restores the value.
The minimum absolute value must be recomputed AFTER the flips.
k may exceed the number of negatives.

complexity.why: the sort dominates. A counting sort over the bounded value range would make it linear.

followups.q: Why does only the parity of leftover k matter?
followups.a: Flipping the same element twice returns it to its original value, so any even remainder is a no-op. Only one net flip can remain.

followups.q: Why the smallest absolute value?
followups.a: The forced flip costs twice that value, so you minimise the loss by choosing the smallest.

problems.title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

learnings.insight: Identical to interval scheduling. Shooting at the earliest END point bursts every balloon that overlaps there and leaves the most room for the rest - so sort by end, not by start.
learnings.trick: Sort by end. Keep the position of the last arrow; when a balloon starts after it, fire a new arrow at that balloon's end.
edge_cases: Touching balloons at a shared coordinate are burst by one arrow - use > not >= for the new-arrow test.
Coordinates reach INT_MAX, so sorting by end must not compute differences.
A single balloon needs one arrow.

complexity.why: the sort dominates; the sweep is linear. This is the same algorithm as Non-overlapping Intervals, counting kept groups rather than removed ones.

followups.q: Why does sorting by end work here?
followups.a: The earliest-ending balloon must be burst by some arrow, and placing that arrow at its end point maximises what else it can catch. Exchange argument as usual.

followups.q: Why must you avoid subtracting coordinates in the comparator?
followups.a: Coordinates span the full int range, so a - b overflows. Compare directly with <.

learnings.insight: A third instance of interval scheduling in the same day, which is the point - once you recognise 'longest chain of non-overlapping things' you should reach for sort-by-end without rereading the statement.
learnings.trick: Sort by the second element. Track the last chosen end; extend the chain whenever the current pair starts strictly after it.
edge_cases: Pairs must be strictly increasing, so use > not >=.
Pairs may be given in any order and are not pre-sorted.
A single pair gives a chain of 1.

complexity.why: sort plus a linear sweep. The DP alternative - longest chain by compatibility - is O(n^2) and unnecessary.

followups.q: Pairs have weights and you want maximum total weight.
followups.a: Greedy fails. Sort by end and use DP with binary search for the latest compatible predecessor - O(n log n). That is LC 1235.

followups.q: How is this related to LIS?
followups.a: It is LIS with a compatibility relation instead of a numeric one. The greedy works here because the relation is an interval ordering, which LIS in general is not.

learnings.insight: The wildcard makes the open-bracket count uncertain, so track a RANGE of possible counts rather than a single number. That range idea generalises to many problems with non-deterministic choices.
learnings.trick: Keep lo and hi, the minimum and maximum possible open counts. '(' increments both, ')' decrements both, '*' decrements lo and increments hi. Clamp lo at 0 and fail if hi goes negative.
edge_cases: Clamping lo at zero is essential - a negative minimum is meaningless, since '*' could have been empty.
hi < 0 means even treating every '*' as '(' cannot balance - fail immediately.
Success requires lo == 0 at the end, not merely lo <= 0.

complexity.why: one pass with two counters. The DP formulation is O(n^2) and the two-pass greedy is an equivalent alternative.

followups.q: Why clamp lo at zero?
followups.a: lo counts the minimum possible open brackets. It cannot be negative, because any '*' that would have driven it negative can simply be treated as empty instead.

followups.q: Two-pass alternative.
followups.a: Scan left to right treating '*' as '(' and checking the count never goes negative, then right to left treating '*' as ')'. Both passes passing implies validity.

learnings.insight: Place the tallest people first. Once they are positioned, inserting a shorter person anywhere cannot disturb their counts, because shorter people are invisible to them. That independence is what makes the greedy sound.
learnings.trick: Sort by height descending, then by count ascending. Insert each person at the index equal to their count.
edge_cases: The secondary sort must be ascending by count, or equal-height people are placed wrongly.
Vector insertion is O(n), giving O(n^2) overall - acceptable at these constraints.
The count refers only to people of greater or equal height.

complexity.why: n insertions into a vector, each O(n) for the shift. A balanced BST or Fenwick tree with order statistics reduces it to O(n log n).

followups.q: Why is the insertion safe?
followups.a: Everyone already placed is taller or equal, so a shorter person inserted before them does not change their count. Their positions may shift, but their counts do not.

followups.q: Make it O(n log n).
followups.a: Use an order-statistic tree or a Fenwick tree over empty slots to find the kth free position in O(log n) instead of shifting.

learnings.insight: You only need to count direction CHANGES. Any monotone run contributes exactly one element to the subsequence, so tracking the previous direction is enough - no DP table is required.
learnings.trick: Keep up and down counters. On a rise, up = down + 1; on a fall, down = up + 1. Equal adjacent values change nothing. The answer is max(up, down).
edge_cases: Equal adjacent elements must not count as a direction change.
Single element gives 1.
An entirely monotone array also gives a wiggle length of 2, not 1.

complexity.why: one pass with two counters. The O(n^2) DP over all previous indices is what this replaces.

followups.q: Why is taking the extreme of each run optimal?
followups.a: Within a monotone run, only the last element can extend the wiggle in the next direction. Taking any earlier one is never better and sometimes worse.

followups.q: Return the actual subsequence.
followups.a: Record indices whenever a counter increments; those are the turning points.

learnings.insight: Only one of the three triangle inequalities needs checking once the sides are sorted: if a <= b <= c, then a + b > c implies the other two automatically. That reduces three conditions to one and makes a two-pointer sweep possible.
learnings.trick: Sort. Fix the largest side c from the right, then converge two pointers over the prefix. When a[l] + a[r] > c, ALL pairs between l and r also work, so add r - l and decrement r.
edge_cases: Adding r - l in one step is what makes it O(n^2) rather than O(n^3).
Zeros cannot form triangles - the strict inequality handles them.
Duplicate side lengths are counted as distinct triples.

complexity.why: n choices of the largest side, each with a linear inner sweep. Checking all triples is O(n^3).

followups.q: Why does sorting reduce three inequalities to one?
followups.a: With a <= b <= c, both a + c > b and b + c > a hold trivially since c is the largest. Only a + b > c is in doubt.

followups.q: Why can you add r - l at once?
followups.a: The array is sorted, so if a[l] + a[r] > c then a[i] + a[r] > c for every i between l and r. All those pairs are valid in one step.

learnings.insight: Each senator should ban the nearest opposing senator who would otherwise act next. Two queues of indices make 'who acts next' explicit, and re-queuing the winner at index + n simulates the next round without rebuilding anything.
learnings.trick: Two queues of indices, one per party. Repeatedly pop both fronts; the smaller index wins and is pushed back at index + n. Whichever queue empties first loses.
edge_cases: The winner must be re-queued at index + n to represent the next round.
One queue emptying ends the simulation immediately.
A single senator wins by default.

complexity.why: each senator is banned at most once, so the total number of comparisons is bounded by n.

followups.q: Why ban the nearest opponent?
followups.a: Banning anyone further away leaves a closer opponent free to act first and ban you instead. The nearest is the only one that can hurt you this round.

followups.q: Three parties instead of two.
followups.a: The greedy breaks down - with three, banning the nearest may help the third party more than yourself. It becomes a game-theory problem.

learnings.insight: Prefer extending an existing run over starting a new one, because a run of length 1 or 2 is invalid and must eventually be extended anyway. Two counters - available values and runs ending here - express that without any search.
learnings.trick: Count frequencies. Keep a map of runs ending at each value. For each x in order, extend a run ending at x-1 if one exists; otherwise start a new run needing x+1 and x+2, failing if either is unavailable.
edge_cases: Runs must be length 3 or more, which is why starting a run consumes three values at once.
Extending must be preferred over starting, or you strand short runs.
Values must be processed in ascending order.

complexity.why: one pass over the sorted values with constant-time map operations.

followups.q: Why prefer extending?
followups.a: A run you decline to extend must later reach length 3 on its own, consuming values that the existing run would have used anyway. Extending is never worse.

learnings.insight: n reaches 1e15, so nothing can be enumerated. Even positions have 5 choices and odd positions have 4, so the answer is 5^ceil(n/2) * 4^floor(n/2) - a pure counting problem solved with modular exponentiation.
learnings.trick: Count the even and odd positions separately, then combine with binary exponentiation modulo 1e9+7. Everything must be long long, including the intermediate multiply.
edge_cases: a * a in the exponentiation overflows unless both are long long and reduced each step.
n = 1 gives 5 - a single even position.
The modulus is 1e9+7, whose square fits in 64 bits, which is why it was chosen.

complexity.why: two modular exponentiations, each halving the exponent. Any enumeration is impossible at n = 1e15.

followups.q: Derive the counts.
followups.a: Even indices take digits 0,2,4,6,8 - five options. Odd indices take primes 2,3,5,7 - four. Positions are independent, so the counts multiply.

followups.q: Why does 'answer modulo 1e9+7' signal a counting problem?
followups.a: The modulus exists because the true answer is astronomically large. That only happens when you are counting configurations rather than constructing one.
